title: Falling: why heavy and light things land together

summary.text: Drop a full bottle of water and a bottle with only a little water together, and they land with one thud. Gravity, the force that makes things fall, pulls harder on the full bottle, because it has more mass. But more mass also needs a bigger pull to speed up, and the two match exactly. So both fall in the same way. Only air resistance, the push of the air, slows light, spread-out things like feathers and flat paper. People believed heavy things fall faster for nearly two thousand years, until careful tests showed they do not. The unit then goes further: everything with mass attracts everything else, gravity bends light and slows clocks, and nobody yet knows what gravity is deep down.
summary.art: A child on a balcony letting go of a full and a nearly empty plastic bottle at the same moment, both falling side by side, with a faint bent grid of space-time drawn behind the Earth in the sky.

intro.hook: Hold a big potato in one hand and a small lemon in the other. Hold them at the same height. If you let go together, which will hit the floor first? Make your guess, and say why, before you try.
intro.text: In 1971, an astronaut called David Scott stood on the Moon. He held a hammer in one hand and a falcon feather in the other. A camera was filming. Millions of people on Earth were watching. He let go of both at the same moment. On Earth, the feather would float down slowly and the hammer would thud down. On the Moon, there is no air. What do you think happened?
intro.art: An astronaut in a white suit on the grey Moon, a hammer in one glove and a feather in the other, both just let go, the black sky above.

outcomes: I can say what gravity is: the force that pulls things towards the middle of the Earth. I can explain that 'down' means towards the middle of the Earth, wherever you stand.
I can run a fair test to show that heavy and light things fall together. This works when the air does not get in the way.
I can explain that air slows light, spread-out things, and show it with flat and crumpled paper and a parachute.
I can tell the story of Galileo's question. I can say who claimed heavy things fall faster, who tested it, and how we know.
I can explain that everything with mass attracts everything else. I can use the space blanket as a model of Einstein's idea, and say one way it is not like real space.
I can explain that things falling together feel weightless, and that astronauts float because they are falling, not because gravity has gone.
I can give big examples of gravity: light bending, and clocks running slower lower down. I can say how plants and my ears know which way is down. I can say what nobody knows yet about gravity.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. A force can start something moving, stop it, speed it up or change its direction.
terms.example: Kicking a football is a force. Gravity pulling a mango down from a tree is a force too.
terms.art: A child kicking a football on one side, and a mango falling from a tree on the other, each with an arrow showing the force.

terms.meaning: The force that attracts every thing that has mass towards every other thing. The Earth has so much mass that its gravity is the one we feel.
terms.example: A mango falls from the tree to the ground. Gravity pulled it down.
terms.art: A mango dropping from a tree branch with a soft arrow pointing down to the Earth.

terms.meaning: To move down towards the Earth because nothing is holding you up.
terms.example: When you let go of a ball, it falls.
terms.art: A hand opening and a ball dropping, with motion lines.

terms.meaning: Towards the middle of the Earth. It is not the bottom of a page. For people on the other side of the Earth, down points the other way from ours.
terms.example: In Chennai and in Buenos Aires, a dropped ball falls towards the middle of the Earth.
terms.art: A round Earth with little people standing all round it, each with an arrow pointing to the centre.

terms.meaning: The amount of matter in something, which means how much material it is made of. A steel tumbler has more mass than a paper cup of the same size.
terms.example: An elephant has more mass than a cat. A brick has more mass than a sponge.
terms.art: A brick and a sponge of the same size on a see-saw, the brick side down.

terms.meaning: The force of gravity on something. A thing with more mass has more weight, because the Earth pulls it harder.
terms.example: A full water bottle has more weight than an empty one. You feel the difference when you hold them.
terms.art: A full and an empty water bottle side by side, the full one with a bigger arrow down.

terms.meaning: The push of the air on something moving through it. It is a force, and it slows light, spread-out things the most.
terms.example: A flat sheet of paper floats down slowly. The same sheet, crumpled into a ball, drops fast.
terms.art: A flat paper sheet rocking slowly down beside a crumpled paper ball dropping fast, little air arrows pushing up.

terms.meaning: A space with no air in it at all. In a vacuum there is no air resistance.
terms.example: Space between the planets is almost a vacuum. Scientists can also pump the air out of a big chamber.
terms.art: A giant empty chamber with all its air pumped out, a feather and a ball inside.

terms.meaning: To go faster and faster. A falling thing speeds up every moment it falls.
terms.example: A ball dropped from a balcony is going much faster at the bottom than at the top.
terms.art: A falling ball drawn at four moments, the gaps between them getting bigger.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know what made the difference.
terms.example: Drop two bottles from the same height, at the same moment, onto the same floor. Only the amount of water inside is different.
terms.art: Two identical bottles held at the same height, one full and one with only a little water.

terms.meaning: A big, light sheet that catches the air. The air pushes up on it and slows the fall.
terms.example: Soldiers and skydivers jump from planes with parachutes. A plastic bag with a toy tied under it is a small parachute.
terms.art: A plastic-bag parachute with a small toy hanging below, floating down.

terms.meaning: Falling with only gravity acting on you: nothing holding you up and almost no air in the way. Things in free fall feel weightless.
terms.example: For a moment at the top of a jump, you feel light. Astronauts in the space station are in free fall all the time.
terms.art: A child at the top of a jump, hair floating up, eyes wide.

terms.meaning: Feeling no weight, because nothing is pushing up on you. Gravity is still pulling.
terms.example: Astronauts float in the space station. Gravity still pulls them, but they are falling, so the floor does not push on them.
terms.art: Astronauts floating inside a space station with a tumbler of water floating too.

terms.meaning: A simple thing we make or draw to help us think about something real. A model always gets some things right and some things wrong.
terms.example: A globe is a model of the Earth. A stretched dupatta with a ball on it is a model of bent space.
terms.art: A child holding a small globe beside a window that shows the real round Earth from space.

terms.meaning: Space and time, joined together. Einstein showed that mass bends space-time, a little like a heavy ball dents a stretched cloth.
terms.example: The Sun bends the space-time near it. The Earth moves along that bend, round and round the Sun.
terms.art: A grid like a fishing net, dented around a glowing Sun, with the Earth rolling along the dent.

terms.meaning: The curved path of something that keeps falling round another thing and keeps missing it.
terms.example: The Moon orbits the Earth. The space station orbits the Earth about 16 times a day.
terms.art: The Moon going round the Earth on a curved dotted path.

terms.meaning: A place in space where a spacecraft can stay in step with two big bodies, such as the Sun and the Earth, as they move.
terms.example: India's Aditya-L1 spacecraft watches the Sun from near a Lagrange point, about 15 lakh kilometres from Earth.
terms.art: The Sun and the Earth with a small spacecraft parked between them, all three on one straight line.

terms.meaning: How fast something must go to get away from a planet's pull and never fall back.
terms.example: To escape the Earth, a rocket must reach about 11 kilometres every second. Your best jump leaves the ground at only 2 or 3 metres a second.
terms.art: A rocket racing up past the clouds, a child's small jump on the ground below.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see. Every atom has mass, so every atom attracts every other atom.
terms.example: You, the Earth and the Moon are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a falling stone to a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: What it takes to make something move, warm up or change. Energy never disappears. It only changes from one kind into another.
terms.example: A stone held up high has stored height energy. As it falls, that energy turns into movement.
terms.art: A stone high on a shelf glowing gently, then falling, the glow moving into its motion lines.

terms.meaning: What our eyes see. Light is made of tiny packets of energy called photons. Gravity bends its path too.
terms.example: Light from far stars bends a tiny bit as it passes close to the Sun.
terms.art: A beam of starlight curving slightly as it passes the edge of the Sun.

terms.meaning: A tiny particle of gravity that some scientists think might exist. Nobody has ever found one.
terms.example: Light comes in tiny packets called photons. Maybe gravity comes in tiny packets called gravitons. We don't know yet.
terms.art: A question mark made of tiny glowing dots floating between two planets.

explanations.definition: Gravity is the force that attracts things with mass towards each other. On Earth, it pulls everything towards the middle of the Earth.
explanations.description: Let go of anything, and it falls: a mango, a pencil, a raindrop, or you after a jump. Nothing has to touch it. Gravity acts across the air, and even across empty space. It never switches off. It pulls on you while you sleep, while you swim and while you fly in a plane. You only notice it when nothing is holding you up. The force of gravity on you is called your weight. The unit on Weight and mass explores that.
examples: A ball you throw up always comes back down.
Water in a river flows downhill, towards the sea.
Rain falls from clouds to the ground.
explanations.art: Four panels: a mango falling, a ball thrown up and coming back, a river flowing downhill, rain falling.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what gravity is.

explanations.concept: Down means towards the middle of the Earth
explanations.definition: Down means towards the middle of the Earth, from wherever you are standing.
explanations.description: The Earth is a huge ball. People live all over it, on every side. A child in Argentina is standing almost upside down compared with you. But she does not fall off. For her, down is towards the middle of the Earth, just as it is for you. So 'down' is not one direction in space. It points to the middle of the Earth from wherever you are. Builders use a plumb line, a weight on a string, to find down. The string points almost exactly towards the middle of the Earth.
examples: A plumb line hangs straight down. Masons use it to build walls that stand straight.
Imagine digging straight down from India, through the middle of the Earth. You would come out in the Pacific Ocean, west of South America. Nobody can really dig that deep.
explanations.art: A round Earth with children standing in India, Argentina and on both sides, each with an arrow pointing to the centre, and a plumb line hanging from a mason's hand.
explanations.context: Why don't people on the other side of the Earth fall off? This card explains what 'down' really means.

explanations.definition: If there is no air in the way, all things fall in the same way. Heavy and light things, dropped together from the same height, land together.
explanations.description: This is the great surprise of falling. Most people guess that a heavy thing falls faster. Try it with a full bottle of water and a bottle with only a little water, and they land together. Here is why. The Earth pulls the full bottle harder, because it has more mass. But more mass also makes a thing harder to speed up. Think of pushing a full trolley and an empty trolley. A bottle with twice the mass gets twice the pull, but it also needs twice the pull to speed up as fast. So the extra pull is used up exactly by the extra mass, and both bottles speed up in the same way. Only the air spoils this, for things that are very light and spread out.
examples: A full water bottle and a bottle with only a little water, dropped together, hit the floor together.
A cricket ball and a tennis ball, dropped together from a balcony, land together.
On the Moon, with no air, a hammer and a feather land together.
explanations.art: A full and a nearly empty plastic bottle falling side by side from the same height, both just about to touch the floor at the same moment.
explanations.context: Do heavy things fall faster than light things? This card gives the answer that surprised the world, and explains why.

explanations.definition: Air resistance is the push of the air on something moving through it. It slows light, spread-out things much more than heavy, compact things.
explanations.description: Air is made of tiny particles, far too small to see. A falling thing has to push them out of the way, and they push back. That push is air resistance. A heavy, compact thing, like a stone, is hardly slowed by it. A light, spread-out thing, like a feather or a flat sheet of paper, is slowed a lot. Crumple the paper into a ball and it falls fast, though it is the same paper. The faster a thing falls, the harder the air pushes. In the end, the push of the air can become as big as the pull of gravity. Then the thing stops speeding up and falls at a steady speed. Scientists call this its terminal speed.
examples: A big raindrop falls at about 30 kilometres an hour, about as fast as a bicycle going downhill. Without air, a drop from a high cloud would hit the ground far harder.
Seeds of the semal tree, the silk-cotton tree, float on fluff and can drift far.
A skydiver falls at about 200 kilometres an hour, until the parachute opens and slows her to a gentle drift.
explanations.art: A flat paper sheet rocking slowly down and a crumpled paper ball dropping straight, with small air arrows pushing up under the flat sheet.
explanations.context: Why does a feather float down slowly but a stone drops fast? This card explains the part the air plays.

explanations.concept: Who first found that heavy and light fall together?
explanations.description: Everyone now agrees on the answer. But who should get the credit? Many people found pieces of it, over two thousand years. Each one had to argue against what everyone believed.
examples: Aristotle said a stone ten times heavier falls ten times faster. People believed him for about 1,900 years.
Galileo's books made the idea famous, but others had tested it before him.

perspectives.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 2,350 years ago
perspectives.explanation: Heavy things fall faster, in proportion to their weight. He reasoned about it, but did not test it carefully. For a long time almost everyone agreed with him.

perspectives.who: John Philoponus, a scholar in Alexandria, Egypt, about 1,500 years ago
perspectives.explanation: He dropped two weights, one many times heavier, from the same height. The difference in time was very small. So Aristotle was wrong. Few people listened.

perspectives.who: Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot, in Delft, in the Netherlands, in 1586
perspectives.explanation: They dropped two lead balls, one ten times heavier, from a church tower about 10 metres high. The two thuds on a board below sounded as one.

perspectives.who: Galileo Galilei, in Italy, from about 1590 to 1638
perspectives.explanation: He gave the clearest argument. He slowed falling down with ramps to measure it. He wrote books that many people read. The famous Leaning Tower of Pisa story comes from his student. It may not have happened.

explanations.art: A timeline of falling stones: Aristotle teaching in Athens, Philoponus on a roof in Alexandria, Stevin dropping lead balls from a church tower in Delft, Galileo with a ramp, and an astronaut on the Moon.
explanations.context: This card is about the history of one question: do heavy things fall faster? Several people found the answer, and they argued about it for centuries.

explanations.definition: A thought experiment is an experiment you do only in your mind, by careful reasoning. Galileo used one to show that heavy and light things must fall together.
explanations.description: Galileo showed Aristotle was wrong without dropping anything at all. Imagine a heavy stone and a light stone. Aristotle says the heavy one falls fast and the light one falls slowly. Now tie them together with a string. The slow light stone should hold the heavy one back. So the pair should fall slower than the heavy stone alone. But the pair is heavier than the heavy stone alone. So, by Aristotle's rule, it should fall faster. It cannot be both slower and faster. So the rule must be wrong. Galileo wrote this in a book in 1638.
examples: Tie a heavy stone and a light stone together. Do they fall faster, slower, or the same?
Einstein also loved thought experiments. He imagined riding on a beam of light.
explanations.art: Two stones, one big and one small, tied together with a string, falling, with a puzzled question mark above them.
explanations.context: Can you prove an idea wrong just by thinking? This card shows how Galileo did it with two imaginary stones tied together.

explanations.definition: A falling thing speeds up as it falls. Without air, it gains about 10 metres a second of speed every second.
explanations.description: A dropped ball does not fall at one steady speed. Every second, it goes faster. After 1 second, it has fallen about 5 metres. After 2 seconds, about 20 metres. After 3 seconds, about 45 metres. Galileo found this pattern. Falling was too fast to measure, so he slowed it down. He rolled balls down a long, gentle ramp. He timed them with a water clock, by weighing the water that ran out. The distances from the start went up as 1, 4, 9, 16, the square numbers. Where does the speed come from? A thing held up high has stored energy. As it falls, that stored energy turns into movement energy.
examples: Drop a ball from a step, then from a balcony. It hits much harder from higher up.
Water falling over a high waterfall, like Jog Falls in Karnataka, hits the pool below with a roar.
explanations.art: A ball falling past a tall building, drawn every second, with the gaps between the balls getting bigger and bigger.
explanations.context: Does a falling thing go at one speed all the way down? This card shows that it speeds up, and how Galileo measured it with a ramp.

chart.title: How far a dropped stone has fallen, second by second (without air)
chart.note: These are rounded numbers. The stone falls 5 metres in the first second, but 45 metres in the first 3 seconds.

explanations.definition: Every thing that has mass attracts every other thing that has mass. Bigger masses attract more strongly, and the force gets weaker with distance.
explanations.description: The Earth pulls you, and you pull the Earth just as hard. When you jump, the Earth moves up towards you a tiny bit. It is far too little to notice, because the Earth has so much more mass than you. You also attract the Moon, and your pencil attracts your eraser. Every atom in the universe attracts every other atom. Isaac Newton wrote this law in a book in 1687. He showed that the force that drops an apple is the same force that keeps the Moon going round the Earth. In 1798, Henry Cavendish measured the tiny force between big lead balls and small ones, in a building at his home in London. Gravity is a very weak force. A small fridge magnet can lift a paper clip against the gravity of the whole Earth.
examples: The Moon pulls on the sea and makes the tides.
Two people sitting next to each other pull on each other, but far too weakly to feel.
A fridge magnet holds up a paper clip, beating the gravity of the whole Earth.
explanations.art: A child and the Earth with two equal arrows pulling towards each other, the Earth's arrow labelled with a tiny wobble.
explanations.context: Is it only the Earth that pulls? This card explains that everything with mass pulls on everything else, even you.

explanations.concept: Gurutva: old Indian ideas about falling
explanations.description: Long before Newton, thinkers in India asked why things fall. Their words still live in our languages. Guru means heavy in Sanskrit. A guru is a teacher with 'weight'. Gurutva means heaviness. Gurutvakarshan, the attraction of heaviness, is the Hindi word for gravity today. How much did these thinkers really know? Historians argue about it.
examples: Gurutvakarshan is the Hindi word for gravity.
The English word gravity comes from the Latin gravis, which means heavy. So does grave, when it means serious.

perspectives.who: Kanada, a thinker of the Vaisheshika school, more than 2,000 years ago
perspectives.explanation: Things fall because they have gurutva, heaviness, when nothing holds them up.
Bodies fall towards the Earth because it is the Earth's nature to attract them. In the same way, it is water's nature to flow.

perspectives.who: Bhaskara II, an astronomer, in the 1100s
perspectives.explanation: The Earth has a power of attraction, and pulls heavy things to itself.

These thinkers clearly said the Earth attracts things. But they did not say how strong the pull is, or show that the same pull holds the Moon. That was Newton's step. Some modern claims go further than the old books say.

explanations.art: An old palm-leaf manuscript with Sanskrit writing, a stone falling beside it, and the word gurutva glowing.
explanations.context: This card is about what ancient Indian thinkers wrote about falling. People still argue about how much they knew.

explanations.concept: Einstein's picture: mass bends space and time
explanations.definition: General relativity is Einstein's theory of gravity. Mass and energy bend space and time together, and a falling thing moves along the straightest path it can through that bent space-time.
explanations.description: Newton described gravity as a force: the Earth pulls the Moon, and the Moon pulls the Earth. In 1915, Albert Einstein gave a different picture, called general relativity. Space and time are joined together, and scientists call them space-time. Mass bends space-time. In Einstein's picture, a falling thing is not being pushed or pulled at all. It moves along the straightest path it can, through bent space-time. That would explain why everything falls in the same way, heavy or light: the path belongs to the place, not to the thing. A heavy ball on a stretched cloth is a model of this. Like every model, it is wrong in places. The ball only dents the cloth because the Earth's gravity pulls it down, so the model uses gravity to explain gravity. And real space-time bends in every direction at once, not just downwards like a cloth.
examples: Put a heavy ball on a stretched dupatta. A marble rolled past it curves in towards the dent.
The Earth goes round the Sun along the bend the Sun makes in space-time.

perspectives.explanation: Gravity is a force that attracts masses towards each other. His law works so well that engineers still use it to send spacecraft to the Moon and Mars.

Gravity is the bending of space and time. This explains things Newton's law cannot, like the exact bending of light and clocks slowing near heavy things. For everyday falling, both give the same answers.

explanations.art: A dupatta held stretched by four hands, a heavy ball making a deep dent in the middle, a marble curving in towards it.
explanations.context: Is gravity really a pull? This card gives Einstein's answer: mass bends space and time, and falling things follow the bends.

explanations.definition: Things that fall together do not push on each other. So anything in free fall feels weightless, even though gravity is still pulling it.
explanations.description: Ask a grown-up to make small holes near the bottom of a plastic bottle, and fill it with water. Water squirts out. Now drop the bottle. While it falls, the squirting stops. The water and the bottle are falling together, so the water no longer presses on the holes. In 1907, Einstein imagined a person falling off a roof. While falling, he would feel no weight at all. Einstein called this the happiest thought of his life. Astronauts in the space station feel this all the time. Gravity up there is still about 9 tenths as strong as on the ground. But the station and the astronauts are falling round the Earth together. So nothing pushes on their feet, and they float. The unit on Weight and mass goes deeper into this, with the falling bottle.
examples: Water stops squirting from a falling bottle.
Your tummy feels funny on a swing or a giant wheel as it starts to drop.
Astronauts float in the space station, about 400 kilometres up, though gravity is still strong there.
explanations.art: Astronauts and a floating water bottle inside the space station, with the round Earth below and a dotted line showing the station falling round it.
explanations.context: Why do astronauts float? This card explains that falling things feel weightless, even when gravity is still strong.

explanations.concept: Can you jump into space? Escape speed
explanations.definition: Escape speed is how fast something must start out to get away from a planet's pull for ever. For the Earth, it is about 11 kilometres a second.
explanations.description: Jump as high as you can. You go up, slow down, stop and fall back. Jump faster, and you go higher before falling back. Could you ever jump so fast that you never come back? Yes, in theory. You would need to leave the ground at about 11 kilometres every second. That is far faster than a bullet. Scientists call it the escape speed. A child's good jump leaves the ground at only 2 or 3 metres a second. Rockets reach escape speed by burning fuel for many minutes. A small world has a small escape speed. On the Moon it is about 2.4 kilometres a second. A black hole has so much mass squeezed into so small a space that, inside its edge, the escape speed is faster than light. So even light cannot get out.
examples: India's Mangalyaan had to go faster than the Earth's escape speed to reach Mars. Chandrayaan did not need to, because the Moon is still held by the Earth's gravity.
On a tiny asteroid, a hard jump could send you off into space.
explanations.art: A child jumping on the ground, a rocket climbing far above, and a black hole in the corner where even a light beam curls back.
explanations.context: How fast would you have to jump to leave the Earth for ever? This card is about escape speed, from your jump to a rocket to a black hole.

chart.title: How fast you must go to escape, on different worlds (kilometres each second)

explanations.concept: Places that stay in step: Lagrange points
explanations.definition: A Lagrange point is a place near two big bodies, like the Sun and the Earth, where a spacecraft can stay in step with them as they move.
explanations.description: Things closer to the Sun than the Earth normally go round the Sun faster than the Earth does. But about 15 lakh kilometres from the Earth, towards the Sun, there is a special place. There, the Earth's gravity pulls back on a spacecraft by just the right amount. The spacecraft goes round the Sun in exactly one year, the same as the Earth. So it stays between the Earth and the Sun all the time. This place is called the first Lagrange point. The Sun and the Earth have five such points. They are named after the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange, who described them in 1772. Leonhard Euler had found three of them a few years earlier. India's Aditya-L1 was launched in September 2023 to watch the Sun from near the first Lagrange point. The James Webb Space Telescope works near the second one, on the far side of the Earth from the Sun. Spacecraft there still need small pushes from their engines now and then to stay in place.
examples: Aditya-L1, India's Sun-watching spacecraft, sits near the first Lagrange point.
The James Webb Space Telescope works near the second Lagrange point.
explanations.art: The Sun on the left, the Earth on the right, and a small spacecraft between them on the same line, with dotted circles showing the Earth and the spacecraft going round the Sun together.
explanations.context: Can a spacecraft stay in one place between the Sun and the Earth? This card is about Lagrange points, and India's Sun-watching spacecraft.

explanations.definition: Gravity bends the path of light. Heavy things like the Sun and galaxies bend the light passing near them.
explanations.description: Light has no mass at all. You might think gravity cannot touch it. But Einstein said light follows the bends in space-time too. So starlight passing close to the Sun should bend a little. In 1919, there was a total eclipse of the Sun. Astronomers led by Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson photographed stars near the dark Sun. The stars seemed shifted, by about the amount Einstein predicted. Today, telescopes see whole galaxies bending the light of galaxies behind them. The far galaxies look stretched into arcs and rings. This is called gravitational lensing. The Indian-born astronomer Priyamvada Natarajan uses it to map dark matter, invisible matter we know only by its gravity.
examples: Starlight bends near the Sun, as photographed in 1919.
Giant galaxies bend light like a lens, making rings and arcs in telescope pictures.
explanations.art: Starlight from a far star curving around the edge of the eclipsed Sun on its way to a telescope on Earth.
explanations.context: Does gravity pull on light? This card tells how a 1919 eclipse showed that light falls too.

explanations.definition: Time runs slower closer to a big mass. Scientists call this gravitational time dilation.
explanations.description: This is one of the strangest facts in science. Time itself runs a little slower closer to a big mass. A clock on the ground floor ticks very slightly slower than a clock on the roof. The difference is far too small to feel. Over a whole lifetime, it adds up to much less than a second. But today's best clocks can measure it. In 2010, scientists in the USA lifted one very precise clock just 33 centimetres higher than another. The higher clock ran faster, by the tiny amount Einstein's theory predicts. GPS satellites, which help maps on phones, fly about 20,000 kilometres up. Their clocks run fast compared with clocks on the ground. Engineers allow for this, or phone maps would drift off by kilometres every day.
examples: GPS satellite clocks are set to allow for the effect of gravity on time.
Someone living on a mountain ages a tiny bit faster than someone by the sea. Over a lifetime, it is far less than a second.
explanations.art: Two clocks, one on a shelf and one on the floor, the higher one ticking a tiny bit faster, with a GPS satellite in the sky above.
explanations.context: Can gravity change time? This card shows that clocks tick slower lower down, and why phone maps depend on it.

explanations.concept: How living things know which way is down
explanations.description: Living things feel gravity all the time. Inside your ears are tiny stones, made of the same material as chalk. They rest on tiny hairs. When you tip your head, the stones slide and bend the hairs, and your brain knows which way is down. Plants feel gravity too. A seed planted upside down still sends a root down and a shoot up. Charles Darwin and his son Francis studied this in 1880. How plants sense down is still being studied. The unit on Weight and mass has a project where you watch a root find down.
examples: Tilt your head and you know at once that you tilted. Your ear stones told you.
A potted plant tipped over sideways bends the shoot back up within a day or two.
A falling cat twists round to land on their feet.

perspectives.who: The starch-grain idea, most plant scientists
perspectives.explanation: Root tip cells contain heavy grains of starch. They sink to the lowest side of each cell, like sand in a bottle. The plant feels where they settle and grows that way.
Some plants with almost no starch grains still find down. So maybe the whole cell feels the weight of their own insides pressing down. Both ways may work together.

explanations.art: A bean seedling planted sideways in a glass jar, the root curving down and the shoot curving up, with a tiny zoom showing starch grains settling at the bottom of a root cell.
explanations.context: Your body and plants both sense gravity. This card is about how, and what scientists are still unsure of.

explanations.concept: What is gravity, deep down? Gravitons and the big unknown
explanations.description: Scientists know how gravity behaves very, very well. They can land spacecraft on the Moon with it. But they do not know what gravity is, deep down. The force of electricity and magnetism is carried by tiny particles called photons, the particles of light. So maybe gravity is carried by tiny particles too. Scientists call them gravitons. Nobody has ever found one. They may be far too weak to catch. Einstein's bent space-time works beautifully for planets and stars. Quantum physics, the science of the very tiniest things, works beautifully for atoms. But the two do not fit together. Inside a black hole, and at the very start of the universe, both are needed. That is one of the biggest puzzles in science.
examples: In 2015, the LIGO detectors in the USA caught ripples in space-time from two black holes crashing together. These gravitational waves were ripples of space-time itself, not single gravitons.
Some physicists think gravity is not a basic force at all. It might come out of something deeper, the way warmth comes out of jiggling atoms.

perspectives.explanation: Gravity, like the other forces, is carried by tiny particles called gravitons. Nobody knows how to catch one.
Space and time themselves may be made of something smaller. Gravity might grow out of that. These ideas have not been tested yet.

explanations.art: Two giant black holes spiralling together, sending ripples across a space-time grid, with a tiny question mark among the ripples.
explanations.context: We know how gravity behaves, but not what it is. This card is about the biggest open question of all, and the hunt for gravitons.

agreed.text: On Earth, everything falls towards the middle of the Earth.
agreed.evidence: A plumb line, a weight on a string, hangs straight down everywhere on Earth. In the 1800s, the Great Trigonometrical Survey measured plumb lines all across India. They pointed towards the middle of the Earth, with tiny tugs sideways towards the heavy Himalayas.

agreed.text: Without air, heavy and light things fall in exactly the same way.
agreed.evidence: In 1971, astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, and they landed together. In 2014, a BBC team dropped a bowling ball and feathers in NASA's huge vacuum chamber in Ohio. They landed together. A French satellite called MICROSCOPE tested this in space from 2016 to 2018. Two metal cylinders fell the same way to about 1 part in a million billion.

agreed.text: Falling things speed up, and air slows light, spread-out things.
agreed.evidence: Galileo measured the speeding up with balls on ramps. You can see air resistance yourself: a flat sheet of paper falls slowly, but the same sheet crumpled falls fast.

agreed.text: Everything with mass pulls on everything else.
agreed.evidence: In 1798, Henry Cavendish measured the pull between big lead balls and small ones in a building at his home in London. Scientists still repeat this experiment today.

agreed.text: Gravity bends light and slows clocks.
agreed.evidence: Starlight was seen bending near the Sun during the 1919 eclipse. Very precise clocks run slower when they are lower down, and GPS satellites must be corrected for it every day.

agreed.text: Astronauts float because they are falling, not because there is no gravity.
agreed.evidence: The space station is about 400 kilometres up. Gravity there is still about 9 tenths as strong as on the ground. Scientists work this out from Newton's law, and the station's orbit matches it exactly.

challenging.claim: Heavy things fall faster than light things.
challenging.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,350 years ago. Most children and many grown-ups still guess this.
challenging.for: A stone does fall faster than a leaf or a feather. That is what we see every day.
challenging.against: The leaf is slowed by the air, not by being light. Crumple a paper into a ball and it falls almost as fast as a stone. Without air, on the Moon, a hammer and a feather land together.
challenging.context: This card is about the oldest wrong idea about falling, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: Galileo dropped two balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, and proved Aristotle wrong in front of a crowd.
challenging.for: Vincenzo Viviani, who worked with Galileo in his last years, wrote this story down about twelve years after Galileo died.
challenging.against: Galileo never wrote about it himself, and nobody else at the time mentioned it. Many historians think it is a legend. We know for sure that Simon Stevin dropped lead balls from a church tower in Delft in 1586.
challenging.context: Galileo is famous for showing that heavy and light things fall together. This card asks whether the most famous story about him really happened.

challenging.claim: Isaac Newton discovered gravity when an apple fell on his head.
challenging.for: Newton himself told a friend, William Stukeley, that watching an apple fall in his garden set him thinking about gravity.
challenging.against: Newton never said it hit his head. And people knew things fall long before Newton. His real discovery was that the pull that drops an apple also holds the Moon in the sky. He also worked out the law for it.
challenging.context: Almost everyone has heard of Newton's apple. This card checks what really happened.

challenging.claim: There is no gravity in space. That is why astronauts float.
challenging.for: Astronauts float in the space station, and far out in space the pull of the Earth does get weaker.
challenging.against: The space station is only about 400 kilometres up. Gravity there is still about 9 tenths as strong as on the ground. The astronauts float because they and the station are falling round the Earth together. Gravity also holds the Moon, the planets and whole galaxies together, far out in space.
challenging.context: Why do astronauts float? This card checks a very common answer.

challenging.claim: Indian astronomers discovered gravity long before Newton.
challenging.for: Brahmagupta wrote, in 628 CE, that the Earth attracts bodies the way water flows. Bhaskara II wrote of the Earth's power of attraction in the 1100s. These were real and clear ideas.
challenging.against: They did not give a law for how strong the pull is. They did not show that the same pull keeps the Moon going round. Some claims online go further than what the old books really say.
challenging.context: This card is about who should get credit for the idea of gravity, and what old Indian books really say.

challenging.claim: Gravity is a force, like a push or a pull.
challenging.who: Isaac Newton, and most everyday science
challenging.for: It works wonderfully. Engineers use Newton's law of gravity to send spacecraft to the Moon and Mars.
challenging.against: In Einstein's theory, gravity is not a force at all. Mass bends space and time, and falling things move along the straightest paths through that bent space-time. This also explains the exact bending of light and the slowing of clocks, which Newton's law cannot. Physicists use both pictures, and Einstein's has passed every test so far.
challenging.context: Is gravity really a pull? This card is about two ways of explaining it, Newton's and Einstein's.

challenging.claim: In a vacuum, things float, because there is no air to hold them down.
challenging.for: Films often show things floating around in empty space.
challenging.against: Air does not hold things down. Air actually pushes up a little. In a vacuum chamber on Earth, a feather drops like a stone. Things only float in space because they are falling freely.
challenging.context: What happens to things when all the air is taken away? This card checks a common mix-up.

big_questions.q: If you dropped a ball down a tunnel right through the Earth, where would it stop?
big_questions.hint: It speeds up all the way to the middle. Then what? Gravity pulls towards the middle from every side.

big_questions.q: Why does a heavy thing not fall faster, when the Earth pulls it harder?
big_questions.hint: Think of pushing a full trolley and an empty one. Which is harder to get moving?

big_questions.q: Everything falls in the same way, heavy or light. Is the fall something the thing does, or something the place does?
big_questions.hint: Einstein thought it belongs to the place. In his picture, the bend in space-time is the same for anything that passes through it.

big_questions.q: People believed heavy things fall faster for about 1,900 years. Why did so few people test it?
big_questions.hint: Is it easy to doubt something that every teacher and every book says?

big_questions.q: Few people listened when John Philoponus disagreed with Aristotle. Should we trust an idea because a famous person said it, or because of evidence?
big_questions.hint: What would you do if everyone in your class believed something you had tested and found wrong?

big_questions.q: You attract the Earth, the Moon and every star. Is anything in the universe truly alone?
big_questions.hint: Every atom in you attracts every atom everywhere, however far away.

big_questions.q: Time runs a tiny bit slower downstairs than upstairs. So is there one true time for everyone?
big_questions.hint: Two very precise clocks, one on a shelf and one on the floor, will slowly disagree.

big_questions.q: Is gravity good or bad? It keeps us on the ground and holds the air on Earth. It also makes us fall and get hurt.
big_questions.hint: Imagine a day with no gravity at all. What would happen to the air, the rain, the rivers and you?

big_questions.q: If light has no mass, why does gravity bend it?
big_questions.hint: Maybe it is not the light that is pulled. Maybe the path through space is bent.

big_questions.q: A plant in the dark still knows which way is down. What might it be like to feel down without ears or eyes?
big_questions.hint: Their root cells have heavy grains that settle to the bottom. Plants feel what they sense.

big_questions.q: The word guru means heavy. Why might a wise person be called heavy? What gives a person weight with others?
big_questions.hint: Think of someone whose words you always listen to. What makes their words weigh more?

big_questions.q: Most of the matter in the universe is invisible. We only know it is there by its gravity. How can we be sure something exists if we can never see it?
big_questions.hint: You cannot see the wind, but you can see the leaves move.

story.title: The Weigher's Daughter
story.note: John Philoponus was a real scholar in Alexandria, about 1,500 years ago. He really wrote that two weights, one many times heavier, dropped from the same height, land with only a very small difference in time. Galileo really read his books, a thousand years later. Thekla, her father, the roof and the students are made up. Thekla's argument about tying the weights together was really written by Galileo, in 1638. The story gives it to her.
text: My father weighed things for a living. In the great market of Alexandria, near the harbour where the lighthouse stood, he sat under a striped awning with his bronze balance and his wooden box of lead weights. Wheat from up the Nile, jars of olive oil, bolts of linen, black pepper that came on ships from India: everything that was sold crossed his scales first. Everyone trusted them. 'A weigher has only one thing to sell,' he told me. 'It is the truth.'

I was eleven, and I knew every weight in the box by feel. The biggest was as heavy as a small melon, and so cold in the mornings that it made my fingers ache. The smallest was as light as a date stone. The middle one was exactly a tenth of the biggest.

Most evenings, a thin man in a dusty cloak came and sat on the step beside our stall. His name was John. The students from the lecture halls called him Philoponus, which means the Lover of Work. He was a teacher of grammar, of words and sentences, not a famous philosopher. And he had very bad manners. He argued with Aristotle.

Aristotle had been dead for more than eight hundred years, and he was the greatest mind there had ever been. Everyone said so. Aristotle taught that heavy things fall faster than light things. A weight ten times heavier falls ten times faster. Everyone knew that. I knew it. I had seen a stone beat a leaf a thousand times.
'Have you?' said John, when I told him. 'Or have you seen the air hold up a leaf?'

One evening, he asked my father if he could borrow the biggest weight and the middle one. The big one was ten times heavier. 'And may I borrow your daughter,' he said, 'for her ears?' My father laughed and said yes to both.

So I climbed the outside stairs of the grain store with the Lover of Work, holding a lead weight in each hand. The roof was flat and warm and white with pigeon droppings. Far below, in the empty yard, John had laid my father's big copper pan face down on the stones.

'Hold them out over the edge,' he said. 'Both at the same height. Let go of both at the same moment. If Aristotle is right, you will hear the big one strike the pan. Then you will hear the small one, a long time after. Count the time between, if you can.'

Down in the street, three students in white had stopped to watch. One of them pointed up at us and said something, and the others laughed. My face went hot. I did not want to be the girl who threw stones off roofs with a man everybody laughed at. I wanted, I am ashamed to say, for the big weight to win quickly, so that we could go down before anyone else saw.
I held my arms out. The weights pulled at my shoulders, the big one much harder than the small. I opened my hands.
Clang.
One clang. Or perhaps two, so close together that I could not pull them apart. It was like the sound of two drums struck by one drummer.

'I let go badly,' I said. 'The big one slipped.' John said nothing. He went down for the weights and brought them up again, slowly, because the stairs were steep and he was not young. I dropped them again. Clang. And again, holding my breath, watching my hands. Clang. Never once did I hear the long wait that Aristotle promised.

A pigeon feather lay on the roof by my foot. I picked it up and dropped it with the small weight. The weight rang on the pan. The feather wandered down on the evening breeze, rocking like a little boat, and settled on the stones long after.
'There,' I said. 'The light thing is slower.'

'The feather is slower,' said John. 'Is it because it is light, or because it is wide and soft, and the air pushes up on it? Try this.' He pulled a thread from his cloak and handed it to me. 'Aristotle says the small weight is slow. Tie it to the big one. What will it do?'

I tied them together. I thought about it, with the evening wind in my ears. The slow small weight should pull back on the big one, like a small brother dragging on your hand. So the pair should fall slower than the big weight alone. But the pair was heavier than the big weight alone. So, by Aristotle, it should fall faster.
'It cannot do both,' I said.
'No,' said John. 'It cannot.'

The students had gone. The sky over the harbour was turning the colour of a ripe pomegranate. I sat on the warm roof with the two weights in my lap, tied together, and I felt something I had never felt before. It was as if the floor of the world had tipped a little. The greatest mind there had ever been had been wrong about something a girl could test with her father's weights in one evening. Nobody had thought to try, for eight hundred years.

John wrote it in his book. He wrote that if you let fall two weights from the same height, one many times heavier, the difference in time is a very small one. Not many people believed him. His book sat on shelves for a thousand years.

Then, in a city called Pisa, a young teacher named Galileo found it, and read it, and wrote the name of John the Grammarian in his own notes. And he went out and rolled balls down ramps, and dropped things, and argued, and wrote books that the whole world read.
That night, before we closed the stall, my father lifted the big weight from my hands and set it back in its place in the box. 'Well?' he said. 'Which one fell faster?'
I thought of the single clang. 'Neither,' I said. 'They fell together. Only the air is unfair to feathers.'
My father looked at me for a long moment, the way he looked at a sack of wheat whose weight surprised him. Then he nodded, and wrote nothing down, and closed the box.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the story turns on the single clang. Heavy and light weights, dropped together, land together. The feather is slower not because it is light, but because the air pushes on it. Thekla's tied-weights puzzle is Galileo's real argument: if heavy things fell faster, a heavy and a light weight tied together would have to fall both slower and faster at once, which is impossible. The story also asks a quieter question. Should we trust an idea because a great person said it, or because we tested it? And who gets remembered: the famous philosopher, the mocked grammarian, or the girl who listened?
ask: What did Thekla expect to hear when she let go of the two weights? What did she really hear?
Why did the feather land long after the small weight? Was it because the feather is light?
Thekla tied the two weights together. Why did that show that Aristotle's rule could not be true?
Thekla felt ashamed when the students laughed. Have you ever felt that way about an idea you believed?
People believed Aristotle for about eight hundred years before John tested him. Why do you think nobody tried sooner?

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
Each player has three tokens: HEAVY FIRST, TOGETHER and LIGHT FIRST.
One player turns over the top card and reads it out loud.
Everyone secretly picks a token and puts it face down. Then everyone shows their token at once.
Check the answer together. A right guess scores 1 point. A good reason, about the air or about gravity, scores 1 more point.
If a TEST IT card comes up, everyone guesses first, then you do the test together.
When the cards run out, the player with the most points wins.
games.context: This is a card game about falling. Each card shows two things being dropped together. Players guess which lands first, then check the answer and explain it.

flow.do: 1. Shuffle the 24 drop cards and put them face down. 2. Give each player three tokens: HEAVY FIRST, TOGETHER and LIGHT FIRST.
flow.say: Each card shows two things dropped at the same moment. Guess which lands first. Then we check.
flow.kid: Mix the cards. Take three tokens: HEAVY FIRST, TOGETHER and LIGHT FIRST. Each card shows two things falling. Guess which lands first!
flow.context: This is the first step of Drop Race. It is a card game where you guess which of two falling things lands first.

flow.do: Play the card 'A full water bottle and a bottle with a little water, from a table' as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card: a full bottle and a bottle with a little water, dropped from a table together. Show your token!
flow.kid: Practice card: two bottles fall from a table. One is full. One has a little water. Which lands first? Show your token.

check.q: A full water bottle and a bottle with only a little water fall from a table together. Which lands first?
options: HEAVY FIRST: the full one
TOGETHER
LIGHT FIRST: the one with a little water
check.why: They land together. Gravity pulls the full bottle harder, but the full bottle also needs a bigger pull to speed up. The two match exactly, so both speed up in the same way. From a table, the air hardly slows bottles. Any guess is fine in a practice round. Now you know the secret for the rest of the game.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over a card and reading it out. 2. Everyone shows a token. 3. Check the answer and give points. 4. On a TEST IT card, do the test together.
flow.say: Before you guess, ask one question. Is the air slowing one of them? If not, they land together.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read a card. Show your token. Then ask: does the air get in the way? If not, they land together!
flow.parent: Answers that land TOGETHER: the bottles, the potato and lemon, the cricket and tennis balls, and the stones. Also the mango and lemon, the clay balls, the two tumblers and the two books. Also the elephant and mouse with no air, the tied weights, and the hammer and feather on the Moon. HEAVY FIRST happens only when the air slows the light one. So the coin beats the flat paper, the crumpled paper ball beats the feather, and the fruit stone beats the semal seed. The crumpled paper and the coin land almost together. Two cards are LIGHT FIRST: the toy on its own beats the toy with a parachute, though the parachute makes it heavier. Two cards have no heavy one, because the flat and rolled leaf, and the flat and crumpled paper, weigh the same. There the compact one lands first, so give the point to whoever says the air made the difference. The marble from the table lands later, because it starts higher, not because of its weight. On the jump card, the answer is both: you pull the Earth as hard as it pulls you.

flow.do: Look out for the card about two weights tied together. When it comes up, stop and talk about Galileo's puzzle.
flow.say: Aristotle said heavy things fall faster. So would the tied pair fall faster, because it is heavier? Or slower, because the light one holds it back? It cannot be both!
flow.kid: Tied weights card! If heavy falls faster, the pair should be faster. But the light one should slow it down. It can't be both! So what is true?

good: They all fall together.
Heavy things don't fall faster at all.

flow.think: Galileo proved this just by thinking, without dropping anything. Can you prove other things just by thinking?

flow.do: Count the points to find the winner. Then look at the cards the light thing lost.
flow.say: Look at every card where the heavy thing won. What was slowing the light thing down every time?
flow.kid: Count your points. Who won? Now look at the cards where heavy won. What slowed the light thing every time?
flow.think: If there were no air at all, would any card ever be HEAVY FIRST?

printables.title: 12 numbered QUESTION cards, one for each DO card
items: 1 Which landed first? Why?
2 Which landed first? Was it because the tissue is light, or because of the air?
3 What changed when you crumpled the tissue?
4 Which was harder, up or down? Why?
5 What brought you back down every time? Could anyone jump into space?
6 Why is it impossible? How do birds and balloons stay up?
7 The whole Earth pulls the clip down. Why did the magnet win?
8 At the very top, for a moment, the ball stops. Is gravity still pulling it?
9 Why didn't the paper float away?

printables.title: 12 numbered ANSWER cards, to check with
items: 1 They landed together. Heavy and light things fall the same way.
2 The coin. The air pushes up on the spread-out tissue and slows it.
3 It landed almost with the coin. Same tissue, same weight, but less air pushing on it.
4 Up. Going up, you work against gravity. Going down, gravity helps.
5 Gravity. To escape the Earth, you would need to leave the ground at about 11 kilometres every second.
6 Nothing holds it up, so gravity always wins. A bird pushes air down with their wings. A gas balloon floats because the air around it pushes it up.
7 Gravity is a very weak force. A tiny magnet beats the gravity of the whole Earth.
8 Yes. Gravity never stops. It slowed the ball to a stop, then pulled it back.
9 The book pushed the air out of the way, so no air pushed up on the paper.
10 Straight down, towards the middle of the Earth. In Argentina it points to the middle of the Earth too.
11 Your breath pushed air up against it. When you stop, gravity pulls it down.
12 From the table. It fell further, so it sped up more and hit harder.

flow.do: 1. Make three piles: DO, QUESTION and ANSWER cards, face down. 2. Shuffle only the DO cards.
flow.say: Each card asks you to do something with gravity. After you do it, you answer a question about it. Then we check.
flow.kid: Make three piles: DO, QUESTION and ANSWER. Shuffle the DO cards. Draw one and do it!

flow.do: Take turns drawing a DO card, doing it, answering the matching QUESTION card and checking the ANSWER card.
flow.say: Do it first. Then answer. Then check the answer card. Did you get it?
flow.kid: Draw a DO card. Do it! Read the question with the same number. Answer it. Then check the answer card.

ask.q: Card 8: at the very top of the toss, is gravity still pulling the ball?
good: Yes, gravity never stops pulling.
Yes, that's why it comes back down.

flow.parent: Card 6 is a trick card: 'Make a ball float with nothing else.' Let your child try for a minute. Then read the answer. The point is that nothing stays up unless something pushes it up, like the air or a hand.

flow.do: When card 2 comes up, stop and talk about it.
flow.say: The coin beat the tissue. Was that because the tissue is light? Try card 3 straight after, and see.
flow.kid: The coin beat the tissue! Is it because the tissue is light? Now crumple it and try again.

check.q: A coin beats a flat tissue to the floor. A crumpled tissue nearly ties with the coin. What slowed the flat tissue?
options: The air pushing up on it
Its lightness
Gravity not pulling it
check.why: The crumpled tissue weighs the same as the flat one. Only its shape changed. So it was the air, not the lightness, that slowed the flat tissue. This is a game moment. Keep that secret for the other cards!

flow.do: Count the points. Then ask each player for their favourite card.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Why?
flow.kid: Count your points. Who won? Which card surprised you most?
flow.think: Every card had gravity in it. Can you think of anything you did today that did not have gravity in it?
