items.p: Many people think gravity pulls only on heavy things. A girl lets go of a feather, and the feather drifts slowly down. What does that show?
opts: Gravity pulls the feather too. The air just slows the feather down
Gravity does not pull feathers. The wind pushes them down
Feathers are pulled up, not down
Only heavy things ever fall
items.why: The feather does come down, so something pulls it down. That is gravity, which pulls on everything with mass. The air pushes up on the wide, soft feather, so it falls slowly. Picking 'the wind' is a fair guess, but a feather falls indoors too, where there is no wind.

items.p: Draw the round Earth with four people standing on it: one on top, one at the bottom and one on each side. Draw an arrow from each person to show which way is down for them.
items.a: Four people round a circle, each with their feet on the Earth. Four arrows, all pointing to the middle of the circle.
items.why: Down always means towards the middle of the Earth, wherever you stand. Nobody on the Earth is really upside down.

items.p: Lakshmi lives in Chennai. Her pen friend Sofia lives in Argentina, far round the other side of the Earth. Why does Sofia not fall off into space?
opts: Gravity pulls Sofia towards the middle of the Earth, just as it pulls Lakshmi
Sofia holds on to the ground
Gravity only works in India
The air presses Sofia down
items.why: For both girls, down means towards the middle of the Earth. So Sofia stands on the ground just as Lakshmi does. Picking 'the air presses her down' is a common idea, but the air presses equally from all sides.
items.context: Argentina is a country in South America. It is on the other side of the Earth from India. When it is bedtime in Chennai, it is lunchtime there.

items.p: Before the Drop Race, a girl holds a full water bottle and an almost empty one. The full one feels much heavier. She lets them fall together from the same height. What should she expect to hear?
opts: One thud, because they land together
Two thuds: the full bottle first
Two thuds: the light bottle first
No thud, because the light one floats
items.why: The bottles have the same shape, so the air slows them about the same. Without much air in the way, heavy and light things fall together. Picking 'the full bottle first' is what most people guess. The test is there to check that guess.
items.context: In the Drop Race, you lay a heavy thing and a light thing on a book. Then you pull the book away fast and listen. One thud means they landed together.

items.p: In the Drop Race, we lay both bottles on a book and pull the book away. Why not just hold one bottle in each hand and let go?
items.a: A strong answer says that two hands may not let go at exactly the same moment. Then one bottle gets a head start, and the test is not fair. The book lets both bottles go at the same instant.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing: here, how heavy the bottle is. Everything else, like the start, must be the same.
items.context: In the Drop Race, you lay a heavy thing and a light thing on a book. Then you pull the book away fast and listen. One thud means they landed together.

items.p: A girl drops a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled sheet of the same paper together. The crumpled one lands first. What was different about the two sheets?
opts: Only their shape. The air pushed much less on the crumpled ball
The crumpled one was heavier
Gravity pulls crumpled paper harder
The flat one was a different kind of paper
items.why: Crumpling does not add any paper, so both weigh the same. Only the shape changed. A crumpled ball pushes through less air, so the air slows it less. Picking 'heavier' is a common guess, but no paper was added.
items.context: In Paper That Falls Like a Stone, you drop a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled sheet. Then you drop a sheet lying on top of a book.

items.p: When something falls, the air pushes back against it. This push is called air ____.
items.why: Air is made of tiny particles. A falling thing has to push them out of the way, and they push back. That push is air resistance.

items.p: In 1971, an astronaut on the Moon, where there is no air, dropped a hammer and a feather at the same moment. They landed together.
items.why: True. The astronaut was David Scott, and it was filmed. With no air to push up on the feather, nothing slowed it, so it fell just as fast as the hammer.

items.p: Sort these falling things. Does the air slow them a lot, or hardly at all?
cats: Slowed a lot by the air
items: a peacock feather
Slowed a lot by the air
a coconut
Hardly slowed by the air
an open umbrella
Slowed a lot by the air
a steel tumbler
Hardly slowed by the air
a dry leaf
Slowed a lot by the air
a marble
Hardly slowed by the air
items.a: see items
items.why: Light, spread-out things push against a lot of air for their weight, so they are slowed a lot. Heavy, compact things are hardly slowed.

items.p: Why does a parachute make a toy fall slowly?
opts: The wide parachute pushes against lots of air, and the air pushes up on it
The parachute switches off gravity
The parachute is lighter than air
The parachute makes the toy lighter
items.why: Gravity still pulls the toy down. But the wide parachute has to push a lot of air out of the way, and the air pushes back up. Picking 'switches off gravity' misses that the toy still comes down, just slowly.

items.p: A stone is falling through the air. Show the forces on it. The stone is heavy, so the air's push is small.
items.obj: a stone falling through the air
options: gravity
air resistance
push
floor pushes up
items.why: Gravity pulls the stone down. The air pushes up on it a little as it falls. For a heavy stone, the air's push is small compared with gravity.

items.p: A girl drops a ball from a balcony. When is the ball moving fastest?
opts: Just before it lands
Just after she lets go
Halfway down
It moves at the same speed all the way
items.why: Gravity keeps pulling the whole way down, so the ball keeps speeding up. It is fastest at the very end. That is why a fall from higher up hurts more. Picking 'the same speed all the way' is a common first guess.

items.p: A mason in Hyderabad hangs a small stone on a string beside a new wall, to check the wall is straight up. The string always points towards the middle of the ____.
items.why: Gravity pulls the stone towards the middle of the Earth, so the string shows exactly which way is down. Builders call this a plumb line.

items.p: Why does a feather fall more slowly than a stone? Use the word air in your answer.
items.a: A strong answer says the feather is light and spread out, so the air pushes up on it a lot and slows it down. The stone is heavy and compact, so the air hardly slows it. Without air, as on the Moon, they would land together.
items.why: The difference comes from the air, not from gravity pulling the feather less.

items.p: These four things are dropped together from a balcony. Put them in order, from the one the air slows least to the one it slows most: a flat sheet of paper, a steel spoon, a crumpled paper ball, a fluffy feather.
items: a steel spoon
a crumpled paper ball
a flat sheet of paper
a fluffy feather
items.a: order shown
items.why: The spoon is heavy and compact. The paper ball is light but compact. The flat sheet is light and spread out. The feather has the most fluff for its tiny weight, so the air slows it most.

items.p: Is it true that heavy things fall faster? Three people in Kochi give different answers.

views.who: Paati, a grandmother who grows coconuts
views.says: Yes, in real life. A coconut falls much faster than a leaf. That is what matters when you walk under a tree.
No. Without air, everything falls together, like the hammer and feather on the Moon. The air makes the difference, not the weight.
It depends on the shape. A cricket ball and a tennis ball are nearly the same size, and they land almost together. A leaf is a different story.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Use evidence from the Drop Race or the paper test. Then say one fair point from someone else.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and uses a test: the two bottles landed together, and the crumpled paper beat the flat paper though they weigh the same. It answers back fairly, for example that Paati is right about real coconuts and leaves, because there is air on Earth.
items.why: All three are partly right. Gravity makes everything fall together, but in air, light and spread-out things are slowed. Knowing why is what matters.

items.p: Look at these Parachute Test results. A friend says, 'The bigger the parachute, the slower it falls.' Do the results agree with her?
opts: Yes. Each bigger parachute took longer to fall
No. The small one was slowest
No. They all took the same time
We cannot tell anything from these results
items.why: Small took 2 seconds, medium 3 seconds and large 5 seconds. Each bigger one took longer, so it fell more slowly. A taller bar here means a longer, slower fall. Picking 'the small one' comes from reading a short bar as slow.

chart.title: Made-up results: how long each parachute took to fall

items.context: In the Parachute Test, you make three plastic-bag parachutes, small, medium and large, with the same load. You time how long each takes to fall.

items.p: In the Parachute Test, all three parachutes carry the same load and are dropped from the same height. Why does that matter?
items.a: A strong answer says it makes the test fair. If only the size of the parachute changes, any difference in time must come from the size. If the loads or heights were different, you would not know which one caused the change.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing at a time.
items.context: In the Parachute Test, you make three plastic-bag parachutes, small, medium and large, with the same load. You time how long each takes to fall.

items.p: A small parachute with a toy is falling slowly at a steady speed. Show the forces on it.
items.obj: a parachute falling at a steady speed
options: gravity
air resistance
push
floor pushes up
items.why: Gravity pulls the parachute down. The air pushes up on it. When it falls at a steady speed, the two forces are equal, so it no longer speeds up.
items.context: In the Parachute Test, you make three plastic-bag parachutes, small, medium and large, with the same load. You time how long each takes to fall.

items.p: In the paper test, a sheet of paper lying on top of a book falls with the book, instead of floating off. Why?
opts: The book clears the air out of the way, so the air cannot push up on the paper
The paper sticks to the book
The book's gravity pulls the paper down
The book makes the paper heavier
items.why: Underneath, the book pushes the air aside, so nothing pushes up on the paper. Without the air's push, light paper falls as fast as a heavy book. Picking 'the book's gravity' is a clever guess, but the book's pull is far too tiny to notice.
items.context: In Paper That Falls Like a Stone, you drop a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled sheet. Then you drop a sheet lying on top of a book.

items.p: Look at these results from Galileo's Ramp. After 1 beat the marble had rolled 10 cm, after 2 beats 40 cm, after 3 beats 90 cm, after 4 beats 160 cm. If the pattern goes on, how far will it have rolled after 5 beats?
opts: 250 cm
200 cm
170 cm
50 cm
items.why: The distances go 1, 4, 9, 16 times 10 cm. These are the square numbers: 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3, 4 × 4. Next is 5 × 5 = 25, so 250 cm. Picking 200 cm means adding the same 40 cm each beat, but the marble keeps speeding up.

chart.title: Made-up results: how far the marble had rolled after each beat

items.context: In Galileo's Ramp, a marble rolls down a long gentle ramp. You mark where it is on each beat.

items.p: Galileo wanted to find out how falling things speed up. Why did he roll balls down a gentle ramp, instead of just dropping them?
items.a: A strong answer says falling is too fast to measure without a good clock. A gentle ramp slows the speeding up, but it keeps the same pattern. So Galileo could time it and mark where the ball was.
items.why: Slowing something down without changing its pattern is a clever way to study it. Galileo timed the rolls with a water clock.
items.context: In Galileo's Ramp, a marble rolls down a long gentle ramp. You mark where it is on each beat.

items.p: In the Falling Ruler test, a girl catches the ruler after it falls 10 cm. Her brother catches it after 20 cm. He says, 'I win, my number is bigger.' Who was really quicker?
opts: The girl, because the ruler had less time to fall before she caught it
Her brother, because his number is bigger
Neither, because the ruler falls differently each time
items.why: A falling ruler keeps speeding up, so a bigger number means more time passed before the catch. The girl stopped it sooner. Her brother's mistake is thinking a bigger number is always better.
items.context: In the Falling Ruler test, a helper drops a ruler between your open fingers, without warning. You read the number where you caught it.

items.p: When you jump, the Earth pulls you down, and you also pull the Earth up towards you, just as hard.
items.why: True. Every pull between two things is shared. But the Earth has so much more mass than you that it moves far too little to notice.

items.p: In the space blanket, you swap the heavy ball in the middle for a light ball. What happens to the marbles you roll past?
opts: They curve in less, because the light ball makes a shallower dent
They curve in more
They curve in just the same
They roll away from the ball
items.why: Less mass makes a smaller dent, so the marbles are bent less. In Einstein's picture, more mass bends space more, so its pull is stronger.
items.context: In the space blanket, you stretch a sheet and put a heavy ball in the middle. Then you roll marbles past the dent it makes.

items.p: In the space blanket, a marble rolled fast and sideways goes round the heavy ball a few times. What is this like in space?
opts: The Moon going round the Earth
A stone dropping into a well
A balloon floating away
A rocket taking off
items.why: The Moon is always falling towards the Earth. But it moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing. Scientists call this an orbit. The marble only stops because the sheet rubs it and slows it down.
items.context: In the space blanket, you stretch a sheet and put a heavy ball in the middle. Then you roll marbles past the dent it makes.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one a true fact about falling, or a myth?
items: Without air, a feather and a coin fall together
True fact
Astronauts float because space has no gravity
Myth
A heavier stone is pulled harder by the Earth
True fact
Crumpled paper falls faster because it is heavier
Myth
A falling ball keeps speeding up
True fact
A parachute switches gravity off
Myth
items.a: see items
items.why: The myths are common, even in some books. The facts have been tested, many of them in this unit.

items.p: Your cousin Arjun says, 'Heavy things fall faster. I dropped a stone and a leaf, and the stone won.' Which test from this unit would you show him? Say what it proves.
items.a: A strong answer picks a test that changes only one thing. For example, a flat and a crumpled sheet weigh the same, but the crumpled one wins, so shape and air matter, not weight. Or two bottles of different weight but the same shape land together.
items.why: Arjun's test changed two things at once: the weight and the shape. A good test changes only one.

items.p: In the Egg Lander challenge, an egg in a lander is dropped from about 2 metres. Three friends in Mysuru each have a plan to keep the egg safe.

views.says: Use the biggest parachute you can make. It catches the most air, so the lander falls slowest.
Forget the parachute. Pack lots of crumpled paper and straws round the egg, so the landing is soft.
Use a small parachute and a little padding. A big parachute can tip over and land the egg on its side.

items.ask: Which plan would you choose? Explain using air resistance or a soft landing. Then answer back from another friend's side.
items.a: A strong answer picks a plan and gives a reason: a big parachute makes the air push up more, so the lander hits the ground slower, and padding makes the stop gentler. It answers back fairly, for example that padding adds weight, or that a big parachute can drift or tip.
items.why: Real landers for Mars and the Moon use both: parachutes or rockets to slow down, and legs or airbags to soften the bump. There is no one best plan.

items.p: Aristotle, a famous Greek thinker, said heavy things fall faster. People believed him for about 1,900 years before testing it carefully. Why do you think that was?
items.a: Any thoughtful answer with a reason. For example: he was very famous, so people trusted him. A stone really does beat a leaf, so the idea seemed right. Few people thought of a fair test that changes only one thing.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Even clever people can be wrong, which is why we test ideas.

items.p: A stone is dropped from a high cliff, with little air in the way. After 1 second it has fallen about 5 metres. After 2 seconds it has fallen about ____ metres.
items.why: It is not 10 metres, because the stone keeps speeding up. The pattern is like Galileo's Ramp: 1, 4, 9 times as far. 4 times 5 metres is 20 metres.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: a space with no air in it
falling with nothing holding you up
falling round something and always missing
the steady speed when the air's push matches gravity
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are four key words from this unit.

items.p: The Earth pulls a full bottle of water twice as hard as a half-full one. So why doesn't the full bottle fall faster?
opts: The full bottle also has twice the mass, so it is twice as hard to speed up
Gravity pulls everything with the same force
The air always balances it out
The full bottle does fall twice as fast
items.why: Think of pushing a full trolley and an empty one. The full one needs a bigger push to speed up. The extra pull on the full bottle is used up exactly by its extra mass. So both speed up in the same way. Picking 'the same force' is a common mistake: the pull is bigger on the heavier bottle.

items.p: Everyone now agrees that heavy and light things fall together, if the air does not get in the way. But who should get the credit? Historians argue about it.

views.who: A historian who backs John Philoponus
views.says: He was a scholar in Alexandria, about 1,500 years ago. He dropped two weights, one many times heavier, and wrote that they landed almost together. Galileo read his book.

views.who: A historian who backs Simon Stevin
views.says: In 1586, in Delft, in the Netherlands, he dropped two lead balls, one ten times heavier, from a church tower. He heard just one thud.
He gave the clearest argument, measured falling with ramps, and wrote books that the whole world read.

items.ask: Who do you think deserves the most credit? Give a reason. Then answer back from another side.
items.a: A strong answer picks a person and says what counts most: being first, doing a clear test, or explaining it so that everyone understood. It answers back fairly, for example that Galileo used Philoponus's idea, or that Philoponus's book went unread for a thousand years.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Science is built by many people, and credit often goes to the one who explains it best, not always the first.

items.p: Starlight passing close to the Sun goes perfectly straight, because light has no mass.
items.why: False. Light has no mass, but it still follows the bends in space and time near a big mass. In 1919, astronomers photographed stars near the Sun during an eclipse. The stars looked shifted, as Einstein had predicted.

items.p: Two very exact clocks are set to the same time. One goes on a high shelf. One goes on the floor. After many years, which clock shows the later time?
opts: The shelf clock, very slightly
The floor clock, very slightly
They always stay exactly together
items.why: Time runs a tiny bit slower closer to a big mass, like the Earth. So the floor clock ticks slower and falls behind. The difference is far too small to feel, but the best clocks can measure it. Picking 'exactly together' is what everyone thought before Einstein.

items.p: GPS satellites, which help maps on phones, fly about 20,000 kilometres above the Earth. Their clocks run a little fast compared with clocks on the ground. What would happen to phone maps if engineers forgot about this?
items.a: A strong answer says the satellites' clocks would slowly drift ahead of ground clocks. The maps use exact times to work out where you are. So the maps would get more and more wrong, by kilometres every day.
items.why: Clocks higher up, further from the Earth's mass, really do run faster. Engineers allow for it every day.

items.p: How fast would you need to jump to leave the Earth for ever and never fall back?
opts: About 11 kilometres every second
About as fast as a good runner
No speed is ever enough
items.why: That is the Earth's escape speed, far faster than a bullet. Rockets reach it by burning fuel. Picking 'no speed is enough' misses that spacecraft really have left the Earth, like India's Mangalyaan, which went to Mars.
items.context: In How High Can You Jump?, you measure your jumps and think about jumping off the Earth.

items.p: A small magnet lifts a paper clip off the table, even though the whole Earth is pulling the clip down. What does that tell us?
opts: Gravity is a very weak force. It only feels strong because the Earth is so huge
Magnets switch gravity off
Paper clips have no mass
The magnet is heavier than the Earth
items.why: Magnetism is far stronger than gravity. Gravity feels strong only because the Earth has so much mass. Why gravity is so weak is still a mystery. Picking 'magnets switch gravity off' is a fair guess, but the clip still has weight while the magnet holds it.
items.context: In A Magnet Beats the Whole Earth, you lift a steel paper clip off a table with a small magnet.

items.p: The space blanket makes a dent because the Earth's gravity pulls the heavy ball down. Why is that a problem, if we are using the blanket to explain gravity? Name one more way it is not like real space.
items.a: A strong answer says the model uses gravity to explain gravity, so it cannot show where gravity comes from. It also says one more difference, for example that real space bends in every direction at once, not just downwards like a sheet, or that time bends too.
items.why: Every model is useful and also wrong in some way. Knowing how a model is wrong is part of using it well.
items.context: In the space blanket, you stretch a sheet and put a heavy ball in the middle. Then you roll marbles past the dent it makes.

items.p: Your arm got tired holding a bag still. A door handle held the same bag for an hour and never got tired. What does this tell you about the Earth holding the Moon?
items.a: A strong answer says holding something still needs a force, but a force does not use up energy by itself. My arm got tired because muscles use energy just to stay tight. The Earth's gravity has held the Moon for billions of years without running down.
items.why: A force is a push or a pull. Gravity is a force that never gets tired.
items.context: In A Force That Never Gets Tired, you hold a bag still, then hang it on a door handle.

items.p: A bean seed is planted upside down in a jar. The seed sends a root out. Even upside down, the root turns and grows ____.
items.why: Plants feel gravity. Heavy grains in the tip of the root settle to the lowest side, and the root grows that way. Charles Darwin and his son Francis studied this in 1880. How plants sense down is still being studied.
items.context: Seeds sprout a root and a shoot. The unit on Weight and mass has a project where you watch a root find down.

items.p: Many people think astronauts float because there is no gravity in space. But gravity at the space station is about 9 tenths as strong as on the ground. So why do astronauts float?
opts: They and the station are falling round the Earth together, so nothing pushes on their feet
The station has a machine that switches gravity off
They are lighter than air
The Sun pulls them up
items.why: The station moves sideways so fast that it keeps falling round the Earth and missing it. The astronauts fall with it, so the floor never pushes on their feet. Picking 'no gravity' is the most common myth about space.

items.p: A grown-up makes small holes near the bottom of a plastic bottle full of water, and water squirts out. Then she drops the bottle. While it falls, the squirting stops. Explain why.
items.a: A strong answer says the water and the bottle are falling together. The water no longer presses down on the bottom of the bottle, so it does not push out of the holes. It is the same reason astronauts float.
items.why: Things falling together do not press on each other. Einstein called this idea the happiest thought of his life.

items.p: Imagine a tunnel straight through the Earth, with no air inside. A ball is dropped in. What happens?
opts: It speeds up to the middle, shoots past, just reaches the other side, then falls back
It stops at the middle and stays there
It falls out of the other side into space
items.why: The ball speeds up all the way to the middle. Then it is moving so fast that it shoots past. After the middle, gravity pulls it back, so it slows and stops just as it reaches the other side. Then it swings back like a pendulum. Picking 'stops at the middle' forgets how fast it is going there.
items.context: Nobody could really build this tunnel. It is a thought experiment, a test done only in your head.

items.p: Vera Rubin, an American astronomer, found that stars at the edges of galaxies move too fast for what we can see. Scientists think an invisible 'dark matter' pulls on them. How can we know something is there if we can never see it?
items.a: A thoughtful answer says we can see what it does. It pulls on stars, the way you cannot see the wind but can see leaves move. A strong answer may add that scientists still argue about what it is.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Scientists still argue about dark matter.

items.p: Scientists can land spacecraft on the Moon using gravity, so they know exactly what gravity is, deep down.
items.why: False. Scientists know how gravity behaves very well. But nobody yet knows what it is, deep down. Some think it is carried by tiny particles called gravitons, but nobody has found one.

items.p: Draw Galileo's Ramp with the marble's place after beats 1, 2, 3 and 4. Show how the gaps between the marks change.
items.a: A sloping ramp with four marks. The gap from the start to the first mark is small, and each gap after that is bigger than the one before.
items.why: The marble speeds up, so it covers more ground in each beat.
items.context: In Galileo's Ramp, a marble rolls down a long gentle ramp. You mark where it is on each beat.

experiments.title: The Drop Race: one thud or two?
experiments.question: Do heavy things fall faster than light things?
experiments.predict: Before you drop anything, hold each pair. Guess which one will land first: the heavy one, the light one, or both together. Say why you think so. Write your guess in the table.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, both things must start at the same height and at the same moment. Put both on a flat hardback book and pull the book away fast. Drop them onto the same hard floor. Only the thing you drop changes. Try each pair 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: two plastic bottles of the same size, with lids: one full of water, and one with only a little water, about a quarter full (half-litre bottles are easiest)
a big potato and a small lemon or lime
a stack of ten coins taped together, and one coin of the same kind
a flat hardback book
a steel thali or tray to land on, so the sounds are easy to hear
a phone that can film in slow motion, if you have one

experiments.safety: Drop things only onto a clear floor, away from feet and toes. Use plastic bottles, never glass.

schedule.what: Guess, then drop three pairs of heavy and light things. Listen for one thud or two.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Count how many tries gave one thud, and how many gave two.
experiments.context: This is the Drop Race. You drop a heavy thing and a light thing at the same moment and listen. One thud means they landed together. Two thuds mean one was faster.

flow.do: 1. Put the three pairs on the table. They are the two bottles, the potato and the lemon, and the ten coins with the one coin. 2. Let your child hold each pair, one in each hand, and feel which is heavier. 3. Ask them to guess which will land first, and write the guesses down.
flow.say: Hold one in each hand. Which is heavier? If we drop them together, which one will land first?
flow.kid: Hold the two bottles, one in each hand. Which is heavier? Guess: which lands first? Write it down.

ask.q: Why do you think that one will land first?
good: It is heavier, so gravity pulls it harder.
I think they will land together.
I am not sure, so I want to test it.

flow.parent: Most children, and most grown-ups, guess the heavy one lands first. That is a very good guess to start with. Do not correct it yet. The test will. We use a bottle with a little water, not an empty one, because an empty bottle is so light that the air slows it a little and spoils the test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Drop Race. You guess whether a heavy or a light thing lands first, before you test it.

flow.do: 1. Put the steel thali on the floor. 2. Hold the hardback book flat, at about the height of your chin. 3. Lay the two bottles across the book, side by side. 4. Pull the book away quickly towards you, so both bottles start falling at the same moment.
flow.say: Watch and listen. If you hear one thud, they landed together. If you hear two, one was faster.
flow.kid: Put both bottles on the book. Pull the book away fast. Listen! One thud, or two?
flow.parent: Pulling the book away is the secret of a fair start. Hands almost never let go at exactly the same moment, but a book pulled away does. If you have a phone, film it in slow motion.

flow.do: 1. Drop each pair 3 times, using the book. The coins lie flat on the book. Hold the book level so the potato and lemon do not roll off. 2. After each drop, write 'one thud' or 'two thuds' in the table. 3. If it is hard to tell, film it in slow motion and watch it back.
flow.say: Let's do each pair three times. Listen carefully each time. One thud or two?
flow.kid: Drop each pair 3 times. After each drop, write one thud or two thuds.

check.q: You dropped a full bottle and a bottle with a little water together from the same height. What happened?
options: The full bottle landed first
They landed together
The bottle with a little water landed first
check.why: They landed together, with one thud. The Earth pulls the full bottle harder. But the full bottle also needs a bigger pull to speed up. The two match exactly, so both speed up the same way. Picking 'the full bottle first' means trusting the old guess over what you heard. Try again and listen closely.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Count how many drops gave one thud.
flow.say: Look at the table. Were your guesses right? What did nearly every drop show?
flow.kid: Look at your table. How many drops gave one thud? Was your guess right?

ask.q: Did the heavy thing ever land first?
good: No. They landed together almost every time.
Once, but I think the book tipped.

flow.think: People believed heavy things fall faster for about two thousand years. Why do you think so few people tested it like this?

experiments.title: Paper That Falls Like a Stone
experiments.question: Why does a sheet of paper fall slowly? Is it because it is light?
experiments.predict: Guess first. A flat sheet of paper and a crumpled sheet weigh exactly the same. Will they fall together? What will a flat sheet do if you lay it on top of a book and drop them? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Use two sheets of the same paper, the same size. Change only their shape: one flat and one crumpled. Drop them from the same height at the same moment. Do each drop 3 times.

materials.item: two sheets of the same paper, the same size
a hardback book bigger than the paper
a coin

experiments.safety: Nothing in this test is dangerous. Keep the book drop low, and away from toes.

schedule.what: Drop flat paper, crumpled paper, and paper on top of a book.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the flat sheet falling, and the arrows of the air pushing up on it.
experiments.context: This experiment uses two sheets of paper and a book. It shows that the air, not lightness, is what slows a falling sheet of paper. The air's push is called air resistance.

flow.do: 1. Hold a flat sheet of paper in one hand and a coin in the other, at the same height. 2. Let go of both together.
flow.say: The coin dropped fast and the paper floated down. Is that because the paper is light? Let's find out.
flow.kid: Hold a flat paper and a coin up high. Let go of both. Which lands first?
flow.context: This is the first step of Paper That Falls Like a Stone. You find out why paper falls slowly.

flow.do: 1. Crumple one sheet into a tight ball. 2. Hold the crumpled ball and a flat sheet at the same height. 3. Drop them together. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Both sheets weigh exactly the same. Only the shape is different. Watch what happens.
flow.kid: Crumple one paper into a tight ball. Drop it with a flat paper. Same paper, same weight. Which lands first?

ask.q: They weigh the same. So why did the ball land first?
good: The flat paper has to push lots of air out of the way.
The air pushes up on the flat paper more.

flow.do: 1. Lay a flat sheet on top of the book, smaller than the book so nothing sticks out. 2. Hold the book flat at chin height. 3. Let go of the book.
flow.say: What will the paper do now? Will it float off, or stay on the book?
flow.kid: Lay a flat paper on top of a book. Drop the book. Does the paper float away, or fall with the book?

check.q: A flat sheet of paper lying on top of a book falls with the book. Why?
options: The paper sticks to the book
The book pushes the air out of the way, so no air pushes on the paper
The book pulls the paper down with its own gravity
check.why: The book goes first and clears the air out of the way. With no air pushing up on it, the paper falls just like the book. That shows the paper is not slow because it is light. It is slow because air pushes on it. Picking 'it sticks' is a fair guess. Try lifting the paper off the book. It is not stuck at all.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: paper falls slowly because the air pushes on it, not because it is light. What I saw: the crumpled paper fell much faster than the flat paper, though they weigh the same. Paper on a book fell with the book. Why: the flat paper has to push a lot of air, and the air pushes back.

experiments.title: The Parachute Test
experiments.question: Does a bigger parachute fall more slowly?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will make three parachutes, small, medium and large, all carrying the same load. Which will take longest to reach the ground, and why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the size of the parachute. Use the same plastic, the same strings, the same load and the same drop height. Time each parachute 3 times, because one drop can be a fluke.

materials.item: thin plastic bags, cut into three squares: about 20, 30 and 40 centimetres across
thread, cut into 12 pieces each about 30 centimetres long
3 identical small loads, such as wooden clothes pegs or small toys
sticky tape, scissors and a ruler
a phone stopwatch, or a stopwatch

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with scissors. Drop the parachutes down a stairwell, or from a balcony with a grown-up holding them, and only when nobody is below. Your child stays back from the railing. Keep plastic bags away from small children's faces.

schedule.what: Make three parachutes. Time each one falling 3 times. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each parachute, as tall as its middle time.
experiments.context: In the Parachute Test, you make three plastic-bag parachutes of different sizes. You time how long each takes to float down from the same height, carrying the same load.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts three squares from plastic bags: about 20, 30 and 40 centimetres across. 2. Tape a thread to each corner of each square. 3. Tie the four threads of each square to one clothes peg.
flow.say: We are making three parachutes. Only the size will be different. Everything else stays the same.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut three plastic squares: small, medium and large. Tape a thread to each corner. Tie the threads to a peg.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Parachute Test. You make three parachutes of different sizes, with the same load under each.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which parachute will take longest to fall, and to put them in order.
flow.say: Which one will take the longest to come down? Put them in order, slowest first.
flow.kid: Which parachute will fall most slowly? Put them in order. Slowest first.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up stands at the top of the stairs or on a balcony. They hold a parachute out, open, with the peg hanging down. 2. Your child says 'Go!' and starts the stopwatch as it is let go. 3. Stop the stopwatch when the peg touches the ground. 4. Write the time. 5. Do each parachute 3 times. If you have no safe stairwell or balcony, stand on a sturdy bed and hold the parachute up high. The times will be shorter.
flow.say: Ready? Start the stopwatch when I let go. Stop it the moment the peg touches the ground.
flow.kid: Say Go! Start the stopwatch. Stop it when the peg lands. Write the time. Do each parachute 3 times.
flow.parent: To find the middle time, put the three times in order and take the middle one. If one parachute gets tangled, that drop does not count. Drop it again.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle times, one bar for each parachute.
flow.say: Let's turn the times into a picture. A taller bar means a slower fall.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each parachute. Make it as tall as its middle time. Taller bar, slower fall.

check.q: In the Parachute Test, which parachute fell most slowly?
options: The smallest
The largest
They all took the same time
check.why: The largest parachute catches the most air. The air pushes up on it the most, so it falls most slowly. Picking 'the same time' means remembering that heavy and light things fall together. That is true without air. Parachutes are all about the air.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a bigger parachute falls more slowly. What I saw: the large one took 5 seconds, but the small one took only 2. Why: the big one catches more air, and the air pushes up on it harder.

experiments.title: The Falling Ruler: catch it if you can
experiments.question: How far does a falling ruler drop before you can catch it? Is your writing hand quicker than your other hand?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When someone lets go of a ruler between your fingers, how many centimetres will it fall before you catch it? Which hand will catch it sooner, and why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same ruler every time, with the 0 mark level with the top of your thumb. The helper lets go without warning. Change only one thing: the hand you catch with. Do 3 tries with each hand, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a 30 centimetre ruler
a helper
a table to rest your arm on, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Nothing in this test is dangerous. Use a plastic or wooden ruler, not a metal one with sharp edges.

schedule.what: Catch a falling ruler 3 times with each hand. Find out how quick your body is.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Use the chart in the last step to turn each distance into a time.
experiments.context: In the Falling Ruler test, a helper lets go of a ruler between your fingers, and you catch it. Gravity makes every ruler fall in the same way, so the distance tells you how quick your body is.

flow.do: 1. Your child rests their arm on the table, with their hand over the edge. 2. They open their thumb and first finger a little. 3. Hold the ruler at the top, hanging down between their thumb and finger. The 0 mark should be level with the top of the thumb.
flow.say: I'll hold the ruler. You keep your fingers open, ready. Don't look at my hand. Watch the ruler.
flow.kid: Rest your arm on the table. Open your thumb and finger a little. The ruler hangs between them. Watch the ruler, not the helper.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Falling Ruler test. You get ready to catch a ruler that a helper drops without warning.

flow.do: 1. Let go of the ruler without any warning. 2. Your child catches it as fast as they can. 3. Read the number at the top of their thumb. 4. Write it down. 5. Do 3 tries with the writing hand.
flow.say: Catch it as fast as you can! Now read the number at the top of your thumb. That's how far it fell.
flow.kid: Catch it as fast as you can! Read the number at your thumb. Write it down. Do it 3 times.
flow.parent: Wait a different time before each drop, so your child cannot guess when it will come. Most children catch it between 15 and 30 centimetres. If the ruler slips right through, write 'more than 30' and try again.

flow.do: Do 3 more tries with the other hand. Find the middle value for each hand.
flow.say: Now let's try your other hand. Will it be quicker or slower?
flow.kid: Now try 3 times with your other hand. Is it quicker or slower?

check.q: A light plastic ruler and a heavy wooden ruler are dropped the same way. Which falls further before you catch it, if you are equally quick?
options: The heavy one
The light one
They fall the same distance
check.why: Heavy and light things fall in the same way. So in the same time, both rulers fall the same distance. Only your quickness changes the number. Picking 'the heavy one' is the old idea that heavy things fall faster.

flow.do: Use the chart to turn the distances into times.
flow.say: The ruler speeds up as it falls. In one tenth of a second, it falls 5 centimetres. In two tenths, 20 centimetres. So 20 centimetres means you took about two tenths of a second to catch it.
flow.kid: The ruler speeds up as it falls. 5 cm means one tenth of a second. 20 cm means two tenths. How quick were you?
flow.parent: Your eyes see the ruler move. A message runs along nerves to your brain. Your brain sends a message to your fingers. All of that takes time. That time is called reaction time.

flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: my writing hand is a little quicker. What I saw: the ruler fell 15 cm with my writing hand and 19 cm with my other hand. Why: the ruler always falls the same way, so a shorter fall means I caught it sooner.

activities.title: How High Can You Jump? Can You Jump into Space?

materials.item: a long strip of paper and sticky tape, for the wall
a pencil, and a ruler or a measuring tape
a staircase, and a playground slide if one is near

activities.safety: Jump on a flat, non-slip floor, away from furniture. On the slide, climb up only with a grown-up close by.

schedule.what: Measure your best jump. Climb up and down stairs. Talk about escape speed.

activities.record: Write your three jump heights and circle the best. Write which was harder: going up the stairs or down.
activities.context: In this activity you measure how high you can jump, and feel gravity pulling you back. Then you find out how fast you would need to jump to leave the Earth for ever.

flow.do: 1. Tape a long paper strip on the wall, from the floor to above your child's reach. 2. Your child stands beside it and reaches up as high as they can. Mark that spot. 3. Then they jump and touch the strip as high as they can, 3 times. Mark each touch.
flow.say: Reach up as high as you can. Now jump and touch the paper as high as you can. Let's do three jumps.
flow.kid: Stand by the wall and reach up high. Mark the spot. Now jump and touch the paper as high as you can. Jump 3 times.

good: Gravity pulled me back down.
The Earth's pull slowed me down and brought me back.

flow.context: This is the first step of How High Can You Jump? You measure your jumps on a paper strip taped to the wall.

flow.do: Measure from the reaching mark up to each jump mark with a ruler. That is the height of each jump. Write the three heights down.
flow.say: Let's measure how high each jump went, from your reaching mark to your jump mark.
flow.kid: Measure from your reaching mark to each jump mark. Write down all three heights. Which was best?

chart.title: Made-up example: three jumps, measured from the reaching mark
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: 1. Walk up a flight of stairs, then walk down. 2. If there is a slide, try to climb up it the wrong way, then slide down.
flow.say: Which was harder, going up or going down? Why?
flow.kid: Walk up the stairs. Now walk down. Which was harder? Why?

ask.q: Why is going up harder than going down?
good: Going up, you work against gravity.
Going down, gravity helps you.

flow.do: Talk about escape speed. Could anyone ever jump off the Earth?
flow.say: To leave the Earth for ever, you would have to jump off at about 11 kilometres every second. Your jump leaves the ground at only 2 or 3 metres a second. Rockets get that fast by burning fuel for many minutes.
flow.kid: To leave the Earth, you would need 11 kilometres every second! Your jump is only 2 or 3 metres a second. Rockets burn fuel to go that fast.

check.q: Could you jump so high that you never came back down?
options: Yes, if I trained very hard
Only if I went faster than about 11 kilometres every second, which no person can
Yes, on the Earth anyone can
check.why: That speed is called the escape speed. It is thousands of times faster than any jump. Only rockets reach it. On a tiny asteroid, with a very weak pull, a hard jump really could send you off into space. Picking 'if I trained very hard' is natural, because the speed is hard to imagine. It is faster than a bullet.

flow.think: On the Moon, the escape speed is less than a quarter of the Earth's. Why do you think it is smaller there?

activities.title: The Space Blanket

materials.item: a bedsheet, a large dupatta, or a piece of stretchy lycra cloth
four people to hold the corners, or two people and two chairs
a heavy ball, such as a cricket ball, a big orange or a steel ball
a lighter ball, such as a tennis ball, and two balls of the same size
6 to 10 marbles

activities.safety: Keep marbles away from toddlers, who may swallow them. Use a soft ball if small children are near.

schedule.what: Make a space blanket. Roll marbles past heavy and light balls. Talk about what the model gets right and wrong.

activities.record: Draw the blanket from the side, with the dent, the ball and a marble's path curving in.
activities.context: In this activity you make a model of Einstein's idea of gravity. Mass bends space and time, a little like a heavy ball bends a stretched cloth. Things then move along the bend.

flow.do: 1. Four people hold the sheet stretched flat and tight, at waist height. 2. Roll a marble across it gently.
flow.say: Look. With nothing on the sheet, the marble rolls in a straight line.
flow.kid: Hold the sheet tight and flat. Roll a marble across. Does it go straight?
flow.context: This is the first step of the space blanket. You stretch a sheet flat and roll a marble across it.

flow.do: 1. Put the heavy ball in the middle of the sheet. 2. Look at the dent. 3. Roll marbles past it, some close and some far away.
flow.say: The heavy ball bends the sheet. Watch the marbles. Which ones curve in?
flow.kid: Put the heavy ball in the middle. See the dent? Roll marbles past it. Which ones curve in?

ask.q: Which marbles fell into the dent?
good: The ones that came close.
The far ones only bent a little.

flow.parent: This shows two things. A heavier ball makes a deeper dent. And marbles that pass far away hardly bend, just as gravity gets weaker further away.

flow.do: 1. Add the lighter ball near the heavy one. 2. Then try two balls of the same size, a little apart. 3. Last, roll a marble fast and sideways round the heavy ball.
flow.say: Which dent is deeper? Do the two same balls roll together? Can you make a marble go round the big ball?
flow.kid: Add a light ball. Whose dent is deeper? Try two same balls. Do they roll together? Roll a marble fast round the big ball!

ask.q: What happened when you rolled a marble fast and sideways?
good: It went round the ball once or twice before falling in.
It was like the Moon going round the Earth.

flow.parent: A stretchy cloth works best. On a bedsheet, a marble may only curve in towards the ball and not go round it. That is fine: the curve is the point.

flow.do: Talk about Einstein's idea.
flow.say: The dent changed the path of the marble. Einstein said mass changes the shape of space and time in a similar way. Falling things follow that shape.
flow.kid: Einstein said heavy things bend space and time. Falling things follow the bend, like the marble followed the dent.

check.q: In the space blanket, why did the marble roll towards the heavy ball?
options: The heavy ball pulled it with an invisible rope
It rolled down into the dent the heavy ball made
The heavy ball is a magnet
check.why: The marble rolled down into the dent, so the shape of the sheet changed its path. Einstein said gravity works a little like this: mass bends space-time, and falling things follow the bends. On the sheet, it is the Earth's gravity that makes the marble roll down the dent. That is one way the model is not like real space. Picking 'an invisible rope' is close to Newton's picture of a force acting across space. It works well, but Einstein's picture explains even more.

flow.do: Ask what the model gets wrong.
flow.say: Every model is wrong somewhere. What made the ball sink into the sheet in the first place? And is real space flat like a sheet?
flow.kid: Every model gets something wrong. What made the ball sink into the sheet? Is real space flat like a sheet?
flow.parent: Good answers: the Earth's gravity pulled the ball into the sheet, so the model uses gravity to explain gravity. Real space is all around us, in every direction. So the real 'dent' goes inwards from every side, towards the middle of the Earth. The blanket helps us imagine, but space is not really like a blanket.
flow.think: Can you think of a better model of bent space? What would it need?

activities.title: A Force That Never Gets Tired

materials.item: a cloth bag with two full half-litre water bottles in it
a dupatta
a door with a strong handle

activities.safety: Pull gently and steadily. Never yank. Close the door before you tie the dupatta to its handle, so it cannot swing.

schedule.what: Hold a bag still until your arm is tired, then let a door handle hold it. Talk about the Earth and the Moon.

activities.record: Draw your arm holding the bag, and the door handle holding the bag. Write which one got tired, and why.
activities.context: In this activity you compare your arm with a door handle. Both can hold a bag still, but only one gets tired. It shows that a force can hold something without using up energy, as gravity does with the Moon.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the bag of water bottles out at arm's length, keeping it still. 2. Count to 60 together.
flow.say: Hold the bag out straight, and keep it still. Is it getting harder?
flow.kid: Hold the bag out straight. Keep it still while you count to 60. Is it getting harder?

ask.q: The bag did not move. So why did your arm get tired?
good: My muscles had to keep working to hold it up.
Holding it still was still hard work for my arm.

flow.parent: Muscles use energy all the time just to stay tight, even when the bag does not move. That is why the arm gets tired.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Force That Never Gets Tired. You hold a bag still and feel your arm get tired.

flow.do: Hang the same bag on a door handle. Leave it there while you do the next steps.
flow.say: The door handle is holding up the same bag, with the same force as your arm. Will the handle get tired?
flow.kid: Hang the bag on a door handle. Will the handle get tired?

flow.do: 1. Close the door and tie the dupatta to its handle. 2. Your child pulls the dupatta gently and steadily, without moving. 3. Then untie it. You hold one end, your child holds the other, and you both pull equally, so nobody moves.
flow.say: The door pulls back just as hard as you pull. So do I, when we pull equally. Which of us gets tired?
flow.kid: Pull the dupatta tied to the door. Then pull against a grown-up. Who gets tired?

check.q: You pull a dupatta tied to a door, and nothing moves. The door pulls back just as hard. Does the door use up energy?
options: No. Holding still needs a force, but it does not use up energy
Yes, just as much as you do
Yes, but it gets tired more slowly
check.why: The door pulls back with a force as big as yours, but nothing moves, so no energy is used up. You get tired because your muscles use energy just to stay tight. Picking 'just as much as you do' is a fair guess, because the forces are equal. But the energy is used inside your muscles, not by the force itself.

flow.parent: Against the door, only your child gets tired. Against you, you both get tired, because both of you are keeping your muscles tight. The door holds the pull without using up energy.

flow.do: Talk about the Earth and the Moon.
flow.say: The Earth's gravity has kept the Moon going round it for more than four billion years. Like the door handle, gravity does not get tired.
flow.kid: The Earth has kept the Moon going round it for billions of years. Gravity never gets tired, like the door handle.
flow.parent: Holding something still, or swinging it steadily round in a circle, takes a force but uses up no energy. That is why the Earth's gravity can keep the Moon going round without running down.
flow.think: Look at the bag on the door handle. Could the handle hold it for a whole year?

activities.title: Which Way Is Down?

materials.item: a piece of thread about as long as your arm, and a heavy nut, a key or a small stone
a ball or a big round fruit, such as an orange
paper, a pencil, scissors and sticky tape

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Make a plumb line and test walls. Stick paper people all round a ball.

activities.record: Draw the round Earth with four people standing on it. Draw an arrow from each person to show which way is down.
activities.context: In this activity you make a plumb line, a weight on a string that shows which way is down. Then you find out what 'down' means on a round Earth.

flow.do: 1. Tie the nut or key firmly to one end of the thread. 2. Hold the other end still and let the weight hang. 3. Hold it next to a door frame, a wall and a table leg. Is each one straight up and down?
flow.say: This is a plumb line. Builders have used it for thousands of years. The string always points straight down. Let's check our walls.
flow.kid: Tie a key to a thread. Let it hang still. This is a plumb line. It shows which way is down. Hold it next to a door. Is the door straight?
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Way Is Down? You make a plumb line, a weight on a string, to find down.

flow.do: 1. Draw and cut out four tiny paper people. 2. Tape them standing all round a ball: one on top, one at the bottom, one on each side. 3. Ask: which way is down for each person?
flow.say: This ball is the Earth. One person is in India, on top. One is in Argentina, at the bottom. Which way is down for her? Why doesn't she fall off?
flow.kid: Make 4 tiny paper people. Stick them all round a ball. Which way is down for the one at the bottom? Why doesn't she fall off?

check.q: A girl is standing in Argentina, on the other side of the Earth from India. Which way is down for her?
options: Towards the middle of the Earth
Towards India
Towards the bottom of the universe
check.why: Down always means towards the middle of the Earth. For her, that is almost the opposite way from ours, and she stands just as easily as we do. Picking 'the bottom of the universe' means imagining space has a bottom, like a page. Space has no bottom. Down is wherever the Earth's middle is.

flow.do: Draw the Earth as a big circle with four people round it. Draw an arrow from each person to the centre.
flow.say: Every arrow points to the middle. So 'down' is not one direction. It is towards the middle of the Earth, from wherever you are.
flow.kid: Draw the Earth and four people. Draw an arrow from each person to the middle. All the arrows meet!

flow.do: Ask the tunnel question.
flow.say: Imagine a tunnel straight through the Earth. If you dropped a ball in, where would it go?
flow.kid: Imagine a tunnel right through the Earth. You drop a ball in. Where does it go?
flow.parent: The ball would speed up all the way to the middle. Then it would shoot past and slow down, stopping just as it reached the other side. Then it would fall back. Without air, it would swing to and fro for ever, like a pendulum. Nobody could build such a tunnel. The inside of the Earth is far too hot.
flow.think: At the very middle of the Earth, which way would down be?

setup.caption: 1. Hang a key on a thread. It shows which way is down.

activities.title: The Four Sisters' Clocks (act it out)

materials.item: four paper clock faces, drawn and cut out
four players, or one child who moves to each of the four places in turn
a staircase or a sturdy stool for the 'mountain'

activities.safety: The 'mountain' sister stands on a low step, not on a wobbly chair.

schedule.what: Act out four sisters living at different heights, whose clocks tick at different speeds.

activities.record: Draw the four sisters at their heights, with a clock beside each. Write which clock is fastest and which is slowest.
activities.context: This is a short play about four sisters who live at different heights. It shows a real but very strange fact: clocks tick slower lower down, closer to the middle of the Earth.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a sister and a place. The mine sister sits on the floor. The sea sister stands. The mountain sister stands on a step. The satellite sister stands on the top stair. 2. Each holds a paper clock.
flow.say: Four sisters were born on the same day. One lives deep in a mine. One lives by the sea. One lives on a mountain. One works on a GPS satellite, very high above the Earth.
flow.kid: You are four sisters, born on the same day. One lives in a deep mine. One lives by the sea. One lives on a mountain. One works on a satellite, very high up!
flow.context: This is the first step of The Four Sisters' Clocks. Each player is a sister living at a different height.

flow.do: Each sister claps once for every 'tick' of her clock while you count to 20. The mine sister claps slowest, then the sea sister, then the mountain sister. The satellite sister claps fastest.
flow.say: Higher up, time runs a tiny bit faster. Lower down, closer to the middle of the Earth, it runs slower. Let's clap our clocks.
flow.kid: Clap once for every tick of your clock. The mine sister claps slowest. The satellite sister claps fastest!

options: The sister on the satellite
The sister deep in the mine
They all tick the same
check.why: Clocks tick slower closer to a big mass, like the Earth. The mine is lowest, so its clock is slowest. Scientists have measured this with clocks just 33 centimetres apart in height. Picking 'all the same' is what everyone believed before Einstein. It is very nearly true, but not quite.

flow.do: Talk about how big the difference really is.
flow.say: In our play, the clocks were very different. In real life, the difference is tiny. Over a whole life, the mountain sister would be older by much less than one second.
flow.kid: In real life, the difference is tiny. Over a whole life, much less than one second! But the best clocks can measure it.
flow.parent: Be clear that the play exaggerates. The real effect is tiny. For every kilometre higher you live, your clock gains about 1 second every 300,000 years. GPS satellites are very high. Their clocks gain about 45 millionths of a second a day from being higher up. Their speed slows them by about 7 millionths, so engineers correct for about 38 millionths a day.

flow.do: Ask the big question.
flow.say: If clocks upstairs and downstairs slowly disagree, which one shows the true time?
flow.kid: Clocks upstairs and downstairs slowly disagree. Which one shows the true time?
flow.think: Is there one time for the whole universe, or does every place have its own?

activities.title: The Falling Seeds Walk (if you have a park nearby)

materials.item: a cloth bag or a box for collecting
a phone stopwatch
a balcony, a wall or a high step to drop from

activities.safety: Go outside only with a grown-up. Collect only things that have already fallen. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Collect falling things on a walk. Drop them and sort them into fast and slow.

activities.record: Draw your slowest faller and your fastest. Write what shape helps the slow one.
activities.context: If you have a garden or a park nearby, try this walk. You collect things that plants drop: leaves, seeds, flowers and pods. Then you race them, to see how living things use the air to fall slowly.

flow.do: If you have a park or a garden nearby, walk there. Collect things that have already fallen: leaves, flowers, pods, winged seeds, fluffy seeds, a small stone or a fruit stone.
flow.say: Let's collect things that trees and plants drop. Look for seeds with wings or fluff.
flow.kid: Go on a walk with a grown-up. Collect fallen leaves, flowers and seeds. Look for seeds with wings or fluff!
flow.parent: Good finds in India are the spinning winged seeds of the sal tree or hiptage. Look too for the fluffy seeds of semal, the silk-cotton tree, and of aak, the milkweed plant. Also flat leaves, heavy fruit stones, and small dry pods.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Falling Seeds Walk. You collect things that plants drop.

flow.do: 1. Drop the things two at a time from the same height. 2. Sort them into fast fallers and slow fallers. 3. Time the slowest one with the stopwatch.
flow.say: Which fall fast? Which fall slowly? What do the slow ones have in common?
flow.kid: Drop two things at a time from the same height. Sort them: fast or slow. Time the slowest one!

check.q: Why does a fluffy semal seed fall so slowly?
options: Their fluff catches lots of air, so the air pushes up on them
They are too light for gravity to pull
They are made of air
check.why: Gravity pulls on every seed, however light. The fluff spreads out and catches the air, so the air pushes up on it a lot. That slows the seed down, and the wind can carry them far from their parent tree. Picking 'too light for gravity' is a common mix-up. Gravity pulls everything, even fluff.

flow.do: Talk about why plants do this.
flow.say: Why might a tree want their seeds to fall slowly? What happens to a seed that drops right under their parent?
flow.kid: Why would a tree want their seeds to fall slowly? Think about where the wind can carry them.
flow.parent: A seed that drifts far away does not have to share light and water with their parent tree. Over millions of years, plants with slow-falling, wind-carried seeds spread far. The winged seed is a living parachute or helicopter.
flow.think: Engineers copy seeds to design drones and parachutes. What else could we copy from a falling seed?

activities.title: Aristotle on Trial (act it out)

materials.item: a full bottle of water and a bottle with a little water, two sheets of paper and a hardback book, as evidence
a wooden spoon for the judge, and paper name cards for each role
two stones and a piece of string, for Galileo's tied stones

activities.safety: Drop the evidence only onto a clear floor, away from toes.

schedule.what: Put Aristotle's idea on trial, with evidence from your own drops.

activities.record: Write the verdict. Then write the one piece of evidence that convinced you most.
activities.context: This is a courtroom play. Aristotle's old idea, that heavy things fall faster, is put on trial. Players act as the judge, Aristotle, John Philoponus and Galileo, and the family is the jury.

flow.do: 1. Give out the roles: the Judge, Aristotle, John Philoponus, Galileo, and the Jury. One person can play two roles. 2. Make name cards. 3. Put the evidence on a table.
flow.say: Today, a very old idea is on trial. The idea is: heavy things fall faster than light things. Aristotle will defend it. Philoponus and Galileo will argue against it. The jury decides.
flow.kid: A very old idea is on trial! Heavy things fall faster: true or false? Choose your role. Judge, Aristotle, Philoponus, Galileo or Jury.
flow.context: This is the first step of Aristotle on Trial. Each player chooses a role in the courtroom play.

flow.do: Aristotle makes his case. He drops a stone and a flat sheet of paper together.
flow.say: Aristotle says: 'Look! The stone beats the paper. Heavy things fall faster. Everyone has seen it.'
flow.kid: Aristotle, drop a stone and a flat paper. Say: 'See? Heavy things fall faster!' Jury, are you convinced?

ask.q: Jury, is this good evidence? Is anything unfair about it?
good: The paper is flat, so the air slows it.
Two things changed: the weight and the shape.

flow.do: Philoponus and Galileo give their evidence. 1. Drop the full bottle and the bottle with a little water from a book. 2. Drop a flat paper and a crumpled paper. 3. Lay a paper on a book and drop the book. 4. Galileo holds up the two stones tied together and asks his puzzle.
flow.say: Galileo asks: 'If heavy falls faster, these tied stones must fall faster, because together they are heavier. But the light one should hold the heavy one back, so they must fall slower. Which is it?'
flow.kid: Philoponus, drop the two bottles from a book. Galileo, drop flat and crumpled paper. Then hold up the tied stones. Ask: faster or slower? It can't be both!
flow.parent: Help the 'lawyers' explain each piece of evidence in one sentence. The bottles land together. Crumpled paper beats flat paper, though they weigh the same. Paper on a book falls with the book. The tied stones show the old rule cannot even make sense.

flow.do: The jury talks, then the judge asks for a verdict.
flow.say: Jury, what is your verdict? Is the idea true or false? Which evidence convinced you?
flow.kid: Jury, decide! Is the idea true or false? Which evidence convinced you most?

check.q: What is the best reason to decide that heavy things do not fall faster?
options: Aristotle was famous, so he must be right
Fair tests, changing only one thing, show heavy and light things land together
Galileo was more famous than Aristotle
check.why: In science, evidence decides, not fame. A fair test changes only one thing. The bottles have the same shape but different weights, and they land together. Picking either famous name means trusting who says it. Both men were famous, and only one was right about this.

flow.do: Talk about the trial afterwards.
flow.say: People believed Aristotle for about 1,900 years. Few people listened to Philoponus. Is it hard to disagree with someone everyone admires? When should you?
flow.kid: People believed Aristotle for a very long time. Few people listened to Philoponus. Is it hard to disagree with someone famous? When should you?
flow.think: Aristotle was right about many other things. Can a great thinker be wrong about one thing and still be great?

activities.title: A Magnet Beats the Whole Earth

materials.item: a fridge magnet or any small magnet
a few steel paper clips

activities.safety: Keep magnets away from phones, bank cards and small children's mouths.

schedule.what: Lift paper clips with a magnet, against the pull of the whole Earth.

activities.record: Write one sentence: which is stronger here, the tiny magnet or the whole Earth's gravity?
activities.context: In this short activity, a small magnet lifts a paper clip off the table. It shows how weak gravity really is, even though it holds the whole universe together.

flow.do: Put a paper clip on the table. Lower the magnet slowly over it until the clip jumps up.
flow.say: The whole Earth is pulling this paper clip down. Watch what this tiny magnet does.
flow.kid: Put a paper clip on the table. Lower a magnet over it slowly. What happens?
flow.context: This is the first step of A Magnet Beats the Whole Earth. You lift a paper clip with a small magnet.

flow.do: Talk about how weak gravity is.
flow.say: The whole Earth pulls the clip down. A tiny magnet pulls it up, and wins. Gravity is by far the weakest force we know. It only feels strong because the Earth is so enormous. Why it is so weak is a mystery.
flow.kid: The whole Earth pulls the clip down. A tiny magnet pulls it up, and wins! Gravity is very weak. Nobody knows why.

check.q: A tiny magnet lifts a paper clip against the pull of the whole Earth. What does that tell us?
options: Gravity is a very weak force
There is no gravity near magnets
The paper clip has no mass
check.why: Gravity still pulls the clip, but the magnet's pull is stronger. Gravity is much weaker than magnetism. It only feels strong because the Earth has so much mass. Picking 'no gravity near magnets' is a fair guess. But the clip falls as soon as you pull the magnet away, so gravity was there all along.

flow.think: Gravity is so weak. So why is it gravity, and not magnetism, that holds planets and stars together?

projects.title: Galileo's Ramp: catching a fall in slow motion

materials.item: a long smooth board, a curtain rod with a groove, or two cardboard strips taped into a V-shaped gutter, about 2 metres long
a few books to raise one end
a marble or a small steel ball
small sticky notes or bits of tape, and a pencil
a measuring tape, or a 30 centimetre ruler
a phone metronome app, or a song with a strong steady beat

projects.safety: Keep marbles away from toddlers. Put a cushion at the bottom of the ramp to catch the marble.

schedule.what: Build a long gentle ramp. Practise letting the marble go on a beat. Guess how far it will go each beat.
Mark where the marble is at each beat. Measure the distances. Find the pattern Galileo found.

projects.record: Write the distance from the start to each mark. Under each, write the difference from the mark before.
projects.context: In this 2-day project, you copy one of Galileo's real experiments. Falling is too fast to measure. So you slow it down with a gentle ramp, and mark where a marble is at each beat.

flow.do: 1. Lay the board or gutter on the floor. 2. Put two or three books under one end, so it slopes gently. 3. Let the marble roll down a few times. It should take about 3 or 4 seconds to reach the bottom. If it is faster, lower the books.
flow.say: Galileo couldn't time a falling ball. It was too fast. So he slowed falling down with a long, gentle ramp. Let's build one.
flow.kid: Build a long ramp with books under one end. Make it gentle. Let a marble roll down. It should take a few seconds.
flow.context: This is the first step of Galileo's Ramp. You build a long, gentle ramp to slow down falling.

flow.do: 1. Start a steady beat, about one every second, on the metronome app or by clapping. 2. Practise letting go of the marble exactly on a beat. 3. Guess: will it roll the same distance in each beat, or more and more?
flow.say: Galileo may have used beats, like music, to time the ball. Some historians think so. Will the marble go the same distance each beat?
flow.kid: Start a steady beat. Let go of the marble on a beat. Guess: the same distance each beat, or more and more?
flow.parent: Galileo really used a water clock, weighing the water that ran out during each roll. Some historians think he also used musical beats. Either way, the beat helps your child feel equal times.

flow.do: 1. Let the marble go on a beat. 2. A helper watches. On beat 1, beat 2 and beat 3, they put a sticky note where the marble is. 3. Repeat 3 or 4 times and move the notes to where they land most often.
flow.say: Watch the marble. On each beat, mark where it is. Let's do it a few times to get it right.
flow.kid: Let the marble go on a beat. On each beat, a helper sticks a note where the marble is. Do it a few times.
flow.wait: Leave the ramp set up for the next day, if you can.

flow.do: Measure from the start to each sticky note. Write the distances down. Then work out how much further each beat went than the one before.
flow.say: Measure from the start to each note. Is each gap the same? Or is each one bigger?
flow.kid: Measure from the start to each note. Write the numbers. Is each gap bigger than the last?

check.q: On Galileo's ramp, how far does the marble go in each beat?
options: The same distance every beat
Further every beat, because it speeds up
Less every beat, because it gets tired
check.why: The marble speeds up all the way down, so it goes further each beat. Galileo found the distances from the start went up as 1, 4, 9, 16. A falling thing does the same, only much faster. Picking 'the same distance' means picturing falling at one steady speed. Picking 'gets tired' misses that gravity keeps pulling the marble, so it keeps speeding up.

chart.title: Made-up example: how far the marble had rolled after each beat
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Real ones will be a little messy, but they grow in the same way.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a rolling or falling ball speeds up. What I saw: after 1 beat it had gone 10 cm. After 2 beats it was 40 cm, and after 3 beats 90 cm. Why: gravity keeps pulling, so the ball goes a little faster every moment.

challenges.title: The Egg Lander
challenges.problem: Drop a raw egg from about 2 metres high without breaking it. Design and build a lander to protect it.
constraints: You may use only paper, 10 straws, sticky tape, one plastic bag and some thread.
The egg must not be wrapped in anything soft from the kitchen, like a sponge or a towel.
A grown-up drops it from the same height each time, onto a hard floor covered with newspaper.
materials: a raw egg (or several, for retries)
paper, 10 straws, sticky tape, a plastic bag and thread
general: A parachute, made from the plastic bag, so the air slows the fall.
A crumple cage of straws, so the straws squash and soak up the bump instead of the egg.
Landing on a wide, flat base so the lander does not tip over.
creative: In 1997, NASA's Mars Pathfinder landed by bouncing on giant air bags. Could paper puffs or blown-up bits of bag work like air bags?

India's Chandrayaan-3 lander, Vikram, landed gently on the Moon in August 2023. It used rocket engines to slow down, because the Moon has no air for a parachute. What would you do on a world with no air?
Winged seeds spin as they fall. Could a spinning paper wing slow your egg?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own lander. Draw it, build it, drop it, and improve it. Can you make it survive from higher up?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. Gravity makes the egg speed up as it falls. Your job is to slow it down, or soften the landing, so it does not break.

flow.do: Explain the challenge and the rules. Look at a raw egg together.
flow.say: Gravity will make the egg go faster and faster as it falls. How can we slow it down, or make the landing soft?
flow.kid: Your job: drop an egg from high up without breaking it. Gravity speeds it up. How can you slow it down?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Egg Lander challenge. You plan a way to protect a falling egg.

flow.do: Each person draws two ideas before building anything.
flow.say: Engineers draw before they build. Draw two ideas. Label which part slows the fall and which part softens the landing.
flow.kid: Draw two ideas first. Which part slows the egg down? Which part makes the landing soft?

flow.do: Build one design. A grown-up drops it from about 2 metres onto newspaper. Check the egg.
flow.say: Let's build your best design and test it. A grown-up will drop it from the same height each time.
flow.kid: Build your best idea. Ask a grown-up to drop it. Did the egg survive?
flow.parent: Hold it over newspaper, at the top of a stepladder or from a stair, about 2 metres up. Many first designs crack. That is good: it shows what to fix. Clean up broken egg straight away and wash hands.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together. Improve the lander and test again.
flow.say: Here is what engineers usually do, and some creative ideas. What will you change?
flow.kid: Read the usual ideas and the creative ones. Change your lander. Test it again!

check.q: Why does a parachute help the egg survive?
options: It makes the egg lighter
The air pushes up on it and slows the fall
It switches off gravity
check.why: A parachute catches the air. The air pushes up on it, so the egg falls more slowly and hits the ground more gently. Gravity still pulls just as hard. Picking 'makes the egg lighter' is a common mix-up. The egg weighs the same. Only the air's push has changed.

flow.think: Vikram landed on the Moon with rocket engines because the Moon has no air. Why would a parachute be useless there?
