challenges.title: The Slowest Fall
challenges.problem: Make one sheet of A4 paper take as long as possible to fall from 2 metres.
constraints: Use only one sheet of paper, scissors and up to 2 paper clips.
Drop from the same height every time.
No blowing, fanning or throwing. Just let go.
general: A flat sheet, which already falls slowly.
A parachute shape, with the paper clip hanging below.
A cone, which falls slowly and steadily.
creative: A paper helicopter: cut two wings and fold them opposite ways, like the spinning seeds of the sal tree.
A long ribbon cut in a spiral, which twirls as it falls.
A glider shape, which slides sideways on the air and takes a longer path down.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own slow faller. Draw it, make it, time it, and try to beat your record.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Gravity pulls every shape of paper just the same. Only the air can slow it. Your job is to get the air working as hard as possible.

flow.do: Time a flat sheet and a crumpled sheet falling from 2 metres. Write both times.
flow.say: Here is our starting record. Same paper, two shapes. Let's time them.
flow.kid: Drop a flat sheet. Time it. Drop a crumpled sheet. Time it. Which was slower?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Slowest Fall. You time a flat and a crumpled sheet, to set a starting record.

flow.do: Make a paper helicopter. Cut a strip about 4 cm wide and 20 cm long. Cut down the middle of one end to make two wings. Fold the wings opposite ways. Put a paper clip on the bottom.
flow.say: Let's copy a winged seed. Fold one wing forwards and one back. Watch it spin.
flow.kid: Cut a paper strip. Cut one end into two wings. Fold them opposite ways. Clip the bottom. Drop it. Does it spin?

flow.do: Try other designs from the lists. Time each one 3 times and write the middle time.
flow.say: Which design falls slowest? Why do you think it works?
flow.kid: Try more designs. Time each one 3 times. Which is the slowest?

check.q: Why does a spinning paper helicopter fall slowly?
options: Its spinning wings push down on the air, and the air pushes back up
Spinning switches off gravity
It is lighter than a flat sheet
check.why: The wings push the air down as they spin, and the air pushes back up on the wings. That slows the fall, like a winged seed. Gravity still pulls just as hard. Picking 'it is lighter' misses that you used the same paper, so the weight did not change.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together, then invent your own.
flow.say: Nature solved this problem long ago with seeds. Can you beat a seed?
flow.kid: Look at all the ideas. Now invent your own slow faller. Can you beat your record?
flow.think: Gravity pulls all the paper shapes the same. So what really changed between the fast ones and the slow ones?

quiz.p: Why does a raindrop fall to the ground?
opts: Gravity pulls it towards the middle of the Earth
The cloud pushes it out
The wind blows it down
quiz.why: Gravity pulls everything with mass towards the middle of the Earth, even a tiny raindrop. Wind can blow raindrops sideways, but gravity brings them down.

quiz.p: Does gravity pull on you while you are asleep?
opts: Yes. It never switches off
No. It stops when you lie still
Only at night
quiz.why: Gravity acts all the time, on everything. It holds you on your bed while you sleep.

quiz.p: In the Drop Race, you drop a stack of ten coins and one coin together from a book. What happens?
opts: They land together
The ten coins land long before
The one coin lands first
quiz.why: Both are compact, so the air hardly slows them. Without much air in the way, heavy and light fall together.

quiz.p: In a fair test of falling, what should you change?
opts: Only the thing you drop
The thing and the height
Everything
quiz.why: Change one thing and keep the rest the same. Then you know what caused any difference.

quiz.p: A skydiver opens her big parachute. What happens next?
opts: She slows down, because the air pushes up on the parachute much more
She stops falling
She falls faster
quiz.why: The wide parachute pushes against lots of air, and the air pushes back up. Gravity still pulls, so she keeps falling, just slowly.

quiz.p: Which of these is slowed most by the air as it falls?
opts: A flat sheet of paper
A crumpled ball of the same paper
A steel coin
quiz.why: The flat sheet is light and spread out, so it pushes against the most air for its weight.

quiz.p: Who said, about 2,350 years ago, that heavy things fall faster?
opts: Aristotle
Galileo
Newton
quiz.why: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, said it. For about 1,900 years, few people tested it carefully.

quiz.p: Falling was too fast for Galileo to measure. How did he slow it down?
opts: He rolled balls down long, gentle ramps
He dropped things in water
He tied them to balloons
quiz.why: A gentle ramp keeps the same speeding-up pattern, but slower. So he could time it with a water clock.

quiz.p: Did Galileo really drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
opts: Historians are not sure. It may be a legend
Yes, everyone saw it and wrote about it
No, he lived nowhere near Pisa
quiz.why: The story comes from his student, written years later. Galileo himself never wrote about it.

quiz.p: The Earth pulls on the Moon. Does the Moon pull on the Earth too?
opts: Yes, just as hard. The Moon's pull lifts the seas into tides
No. A small thing cannot pull a big thing
Only when the Moon is full
quiz.why: Every pull between two things is shared, so the Moon pulls the Earth just as hard as the Earth pulls the Moon. The Earth has much more mass, so it hardly moves. But the Moon's pull is enough to lift the seas a little, and that makes the tides.

quiz.p: In the space blanket, why did marbles roll towards the heavy ball?
opts: They rolled down into the dent it made in the sheet
The ball pulled them with a rope
The marbles were magnetic
quiz.why: The heavy ball bends the sheet. This is a model of Einstein's idea that mass bends space.

quiz.p: You jump off a low wall. While you are in the air, how do you feel?
opts: Almost weightless, because you are falling
Twice as heavy
Exactly as you feel standing still
quiz.why: While falling, nothing pushes on your feet, so you feel almost no weight. Astronauts feel this all the time.

quiz.p: A heavy wooden ruler and a light plastic ruler are dropped the same way. Which falls further in one tenth of a second?
opts: They fall the same distance, about 5 cm
The heavy one
The light one
quiz.why: Heavy and light things fall together when the air hardly slows them. Both rulers are thin and compact.

quiz.p: What did astronomers see during the eclipse of 1919?
opts: Starlight bending as it passed the Sun
Stars falling out of the sky
The Sun stopping
quiz.why: The stars near the dark Sun looked shifted. This showed that gravity bends light, as Einstein said.

quiz.p: How does your body know which way is down?
opts: Tiny stones in your ears slide and bend tiny hairs
Your eyes see the ground
Blood flows to your feet
quiz.why: Inside your ears, tiny chalky stones rest on hairs. When you tip your head, they slide, and your brain knows which way is down, even with your eyes shut.

quiz.p: A galaxy can bend the light of galaxies far behind it. What do telescopes see?
opts: The far galaxies stretched into arcs and rings
Nothing at all
The far galaxies turned upside down
quiz.why: Gravity bends light, so a big galaxy acts like a lens. Scientists call this gravitational lensing.

applications: Masons and builders use a plumb line, called a sahul in many Indian languages, to build straight walls and pillars.
Water tanks on rooftops use gravity to push water down to the taps, with no pump needed.
Hydroelectric dams, like Bhakra Nangal and Idukki, use falling water to make electricity.
Parachutes slow down skydivers, soldiers, supply drops and even spacecraft returning to Earth.
Pendulum clocks keep time because gravity swings the pendulum at a steady beat.
GPS satellite clocks are set to allow for gravity's effect on time, or phone maps would drift off by kilometres each day.
ISRO launches rockets from Sriharikota, burning fuel to fight gravity and reach orbit.
India's Aditya-L1 spacecraft studies the Sun from near a Lagrange point, where it stays in step with the Earth.
Spacecraft use the pull of planets to speed up and change direction for free. This is called a gravity assist, or slingshot.
Engineers test helmets, phone cases and car parts by dropping them from measured heights.
Plants use air resistance to spread their seeds. Engineers copy winged seeds to design drones.
Astronomers use galaxies as giant lenses, because gravity bends light, to see even further away.
Scientists measure tiny differences in gravity to find heavy rock, water and oil deep underground.
Doctors and space agencies study how bones and muscles weaken in free fall, to keep astronauts healthy.
Very precise clocks can now measure height differences of a few centimetres, from how fast they tick.

open_questions.why_open: Scientists can predict exactly how gravity behaves. But nobody knows what it is made of, or why mass bends space and time at all.
Some physicists think gravity is carried by tiny particles called gravitons. They would be so weak that no machine we know how to build could catch one.

open_questions.q: How do gravity and quantum physics fit together?
open_questions.why_open: Einstein's theory works for planets and stars. Quantum physics works for atoms. Inside black holes, and at the very start of the universe, they disagree. Nobody has a theory that joins them.

open_questions.q: Why is gravity so much weaker than the other forces?
open_questions.why_open: A small magnet beats the whole Earth's pull on a paper clip. Nobody knows why gravity is so weak.

Galaxies spin as if there is much more matter in them than we can see. We know it only by its pull. Nobody has caught a particle of it, and a few scientists think our law of gravity is what needs changing.

open_questions.q: Does gravity travel instantly, or does it take time?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists now think gravity's changes travel at the speed of light. In 2017, gravitational waves and light from the same crash of two dead stars arrived almost together. But how gravity really 'travels' is still not fully understood.

open_questions.q: Is anything ever completely free of gravity?
open_questions.why_open: The pull of every star and galaxy reaches everywhere, getting weaker with distance but never quite zero. Even the emptiest parts of space feel a tiny pull.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do plants sense which way is down?
open_questions.why_open: Heavy starch grains in root tips play a big part. But plants with almost no starch grains can still find down, so scientists think there is more to it.

maths.problem: In the Parachute Test, the small parachute took 2 seconds to fall, the medium one 3 seconds and the large one 5 seconds. Look at the chart. How much longer did the large one take than the small one? And how many seconds did all three take, added together?
maths.explain: The large one took 5 seconds and the small one took 2 seconds. 5 take away 2 is 3. So the large one took 3 seconds longer. Altogether: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 seconds.
maths.context: In the Parachute Test, you make three plastic-bag parachutes, small, medium and large, with the same load. You time how long each takes to fall.

chart.title: Made-up results: how long each parachute took to fall

maths.why_maths: Saying 'the big one is slower' is a start. Taking one time away from the other tells us exactly how much slower the air made it.

maths.problem: On Galileo's Ramp, the marble had gone 10 cm after 1 beat, 40 cm after 2 beats and 90 cm after 3 beats. Look at the chart. Spot the pattern. How far will it have gone after 4 beats?
maths.explain: Divide each distance by 10: 1, 4, 9. These are 1 × 1, 2 × 2 and 3 × 3. They are called square numbers. The next one is 4 × 4 = 16. Then multiply back by 10: 16 × 10 = 160 cm. Another way: the gaps are 10, 30, 50. Each gap is 20 more than the last. So the next gap is 70. 90 + 70 = 160.
maths.context: In Galileo's Ramp, a marble rolls down a long gentle ramp. You mark where it is on each beat. The marble speeds up as it rolls.

chart.title: Made-up results: how far the marble had rolled after each beat

maths.why_maths: Galileo found that falling follows a number pattern. Spotting the pattern lets you predict where the marble will be before it gets there, which is what scientists love to do.

maths.problem: A girl jumped three times. Her jumps were 22 cm, 27 cm and 25 cm high. Look at the chart. What was her best jump? How much higher was it than her lowest jump?
maths.answer: Her best jump was 27 cm. It was 5 cm higher than her lowest jump.
maths.explain: Put the jumps in order: 22, 25, 27. The biggest is 27 cm. The smallest is 22 cm. 27 take away 22 is 5. So the best jump was 5 cm higher.
maths.context: In How High Can You Jump?, you mark how high you can reach on a paper strip on the wall. Then you jump and touch it, and measure each jump from the reaching mark.

chart.title: Three jumps, measured from her reaching mark

maths.why_maths: Measuring in centimetres turns 'I jumped high' into a number. Then you can compare jumps, and see how hard gravity makes it to go higher.

maths.problem: In the Drop Race, a family did 12 drops. They heard one thud 10 times and two thuds 2 times. Make a tally chart. Then answer: what does the result tell you?
maths.answer: One thud: 10. Two thuds: 2. Most drops landed together, so heavy and light things fall together. The few two-thud drops were probably uneven starts.
maths.explain: Draw tally marks in groups of five. One thud: two groups of five, so 10. Two thuds: two marks, so 2. 10 + 2 = 12, so every drop is counted. 10 out of 12 is most of them.
maths.context: In the Drop Race, you put a heavy thing and a light thing on a book. Then you pull the book away and listen. One thud means they landed together.
maths.why_maths: One drop can be a fluke. Counting many drops with tally marks shows what usually happens, which is how scientists decide what is true.

maths.problem: In A Force That Never Gets Tired, you and a grown-up pull a dupatta, and nobody moves. You pull with a force of 4. How big must the grown-up's force be? Then you pull with a force of 6. What must the grown-up's force be now, to keep everything still?
maths.explain: Everything stays still only when the two forces are equal and opposite. So your force of 4 needs a force of 4 from the grown-up: 4 = 4. When your force grows to 6, the grown-up's must also be 6. If the grown-up kept pulling with only 4, the dupatta would slide 2 towards your side, because 6 take away 4 is 2.
maths.context: In A Force That Never Gets Tired, you and a grown-up pull the two ends of a dupatta. You both pull equally, so nobody moves.
maths.why_maths: Balanced forces are like a balanced number sentence: both sides must be equal. Finding the missing number tells you the force needed to keep things still.

roots.context: We have been learning why things fall, and why heavy and light things land together. Now we ask what falling tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The Earth pulls a full bottle harder than a nearly empty one, because it has more mass. But more mass is also harder to speed up, like a full trolley. The extra pull and the extra mass cancel exactly, so both bottles land with one thud. With no air in the way, even a hammer and a feather land together, as astronauts showed on the Moon.
deep_truth.habit: We sort things into heavy and light, and expect heavy things to fall faster, because heaviness is what our hands feel most. Falling ignores that difference. Only the air slows some things more than others, and there shape matters as much as weight.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Drop Race, a full bottle and a bottle with a little water gave one thud, and so did ten coins and one coin. In Paper That Falls Like a Stone, a crumpled sheet beat a flat sheet of the same weight, and a flat sheet lying on a book fell with the book.

three.who_am_i: The Earth pulls on every part of you, and you pull on the Earth just as hard.
three.what_is_life: A seed planted upside down still sends a root down. Living things sense gravity and grow with it.
three.what_is_this_world: Without air, a hammer and a feather fall in exactly the same way. Gravity gives everything the same fall.

roots.thread: Gravity does not sort the world into heavy and light. In the same place, a hammer, a feather, a mango and a planet all fall in exactly the same way. Einstein took this seriously. Because every thing falls alike, he said the fall belongs to the shape of space and time, not to the thing that falls. This is a sign that the world is one whole, with one shape that everything in it shares.

teachings.teaching: The thinker Gargi asks what holds everything. Yajnavalkya answers that one unchanging reality holds the Sun and the Moon in their places.
teachings.link: Science names gravity as what keeps the Moon going round the Earth, and the Earth round the Sun. It still does not know what gravity is, deep down. The Upanishad does not describe gravity, but it wondered about the same holding.

teachings.teaching: Kanada, an Indian thinker, said that when nothing holds a thing up, it falls because of gurutva, its heaviness.
teachings.link: In the Drop Race, the bottles fell the moment the book was pulled away, with nothing holding them up. Kanada named that cause gurutva. Guru, a teacher, also means 'heavy'.

science.text: Without air, a heavy thing and a light thing fall together. An astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon in 1971, and they landed together. A satellite called MICROSCOPE found metals fall the same way to about 1 part in a million billion.
Einstein's idea, that mass bends space and time, has passed every test so far. But what gravity is deep down, and how it fits with quantum physics, nobody knows yet.

other_view.view: Aristotle taught that heavy and light are two different natures. Earth and water move down towards their natural place, and fire and air move up. On his view, falling shows how things differ, not what they share.

practice.title: Heavy hand, light hand
practice.say: Sit on the floor with a cushion in front of you. Hold a steel spoon in one hand and a crumpled paper ball in the other. Close your eyes and feel which hand is heavier. Now hold both over the cushion and open your hands together. Listen for the soft landings. Then put your hands in your lap and breathe slowly three times. Feel your heavy bones and your light hair, all held down by the same gravity.

how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, most people believed what the Greek thinker Aristotle taught: a heavy thing falls faster than a light one, in proportion to its weight. It seemed obvious, because a stone does beat a leaf. About 1,500 years ago, John Philoponus, a scholar in Alexandria, dropped two weights from the same height, one many times heavier than the other. He wrote that the difference in time was very small. Few people took notice. In 1586, Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot dropped two lead balls, one ten times heavier, from a church tower in Delft, about 10 metres up. The two thuds on a board below sounded as one. Then Galileo Galilei slowed falling down by rolling balls along gentle ramps, so that he could measure it. In 1638 he wrote that, without air, all things would fall at the same speed. A leaf lags behind because the air slows it, not because it is light. In 1971, the astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the airless Moon, and they landed together.
how_we_found_out.who: Aristotle (the old idea), John Philoponus, Simon Stevin with Jan Cornets de Groot, Galileo Galilei, and the astronaut David Scott
how_we_found_out.when: The 300s BCE (Aristotle), the 500s CE (Philoponus), 1586 (Stevin), 1638 (Galileo's book) and 1971 (the Moon drop)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Aristotle taught that heavier things fall faster, in proportion to their weight. Drops from the same height showed that heavy and light weights land almost together, and Galileo showed that the air, not lightness, slows things like leaves.
